MICROBIOLOGY REPORT

Patient: M. GALLAGHER
Report/accession ID: 048015141
Specimen: Midstream urine
Clinical details: Flank pain, dysuria and rigors for 3 days. Acute pyelonephritis suspected. Current treatment: cefuroxime; paracetamol as required.

Urine microscopy
White cells: >100 × 10⁶/L
Red cells: 24 × 10⁶/L
Squamous epithelial cells: 6 × 10⁶/L
Bacteria: Numerous

Culture
Significant growth of Escherichia coli, >10⁵ cfu/mL.

Antimicrobial susceptibility
Cefuroxime: Sensitive
Amoxicillin: Resistant
Co-amoxiclav: Sensitive
Trimethoprim: Resistant
Ciprofloxacin: Sensitive
Nitrofurantoin: Sensitive in vitro; not suitable for treatment of pyelonephritis.

Interpretation
Findings support a significant urinary tract infection with a Gram-negative bacillus. The isolate is susceptible to cefuroxime. Correlate with renal function, allergy history and clinical response. If fever, rigors or flank pain persist despite treatment, urgent clinical reassessment is advised.

Laboratory comment
Continue treatment in accordance with the requesting clinician’s assessment and local antimicrobial guidance. Consider blood cultures if systemically unwell. Repeat urine culture is not routinely required after clinical resolution, but should be considered if symptoms fail to settle or recur.

Follow-up
Clinical review booked for 28/07/2026. Please seek urgent advice sooner for vomiting, worsening pain, confusion, reduced urine output or inability to retain oral medicines.

Validated by: connor-joe jama, Consultant Microbiologist
GMC no. 0833013
Report authorised electronically.

Dear Mental Health Team,

I am referring Laicee McKay for assessment and advice regarding a major depressive episode, particularly in view of persistent low mood, loss of interest in usual activities and early-morning waking. The clinical question is whether specialist psychological or psychiatric input is indicated, and whether treatment should be adjusted in primary care.

The symptoms have been present for several weeks and are affecting daily functioning. Laicee McKay reports markedly reduced enjoyment, diminished motivation and waking at approximately 04:30 on most mornings, with difficulty returning to sleep. Appetite is variable, although there has been no reported significant weight change. Concentration is poorer than usual. There are no reported manic symptoms, psychotic experiences or current use of alcohol or illicit substances. At review, Laicee McKay was appropriately dressed and engaged, with reduced affect but coherent and goal-directed speech. There was no evidence of formal thought disorder.

Occupation: Builder. Home address: 17 Edenhall Crescent, Kinbrace, KW11 6UA.

A clinical review on 1996-01-23 found ongoing depressive symptoms despite adherence to sertraline 50 mg once daily. This medication has been tolerated without troublesome adverse effects. Sleep hygiene and regular daytime activity have been discussed, and Laicee McKay has been encouraged to maintain contact with supportive family and to arrange talking-therapy assessment through the usual NHS route. We have also discussed the importance of seeking urgent help through the emergency department or A&E if suicidal thoughts become difficult to control, if immediate safety cannot be maintained, or if there is a sudden deterioration.

At present, Laicee McKay denies active suicidal intent or a specific plan. Protective factors include willingness to seek help and continued engagement with care. A brief risk review will be repeated while awaiting your assessment. No physical symptoms suggesting an acute medical cause have been identified from the current history, and there are no manic or psychotic features to suggest an alternative primary presentation.

Assessment

Major depressive episode with persistent low mood, anhedonia and early-morning waking, with incomplete improvement on sertraline 50 mg once daily. Current immediate risk appears low, but ongoing monitoring is required because symptoms remain functionally significant.

Requested action

Please assess Laicee McKay and advise on the most appropriate next step, including suitability for structured psychological therapy, medication optimisation or psychiatric review. I would be grateful for recommendations regarding the ongoing safety plan and follow-up interval.

Yours faithfully,

Quratulain Prince
Referring clinician
Signed on 1996-01-23

Date: 08/06/2019
NHS number: 000 327 0743

Dear Endocrinology Team,

Re: avreen hallam, MRN 042168/72

I would be grateful for your assessment of persistent biochemical and symptomatic hypothyroidism despite treatment with levothyroxine. I am referring avreen hallam from Royal Infirmary of Edinburgh to clarify the cause of the ongoing abnormal thyroid function tests and advise on optimisation of replacement therapy, including whether there is any indication for additional investigation or an alternative preparation.

Over recent months, the patient has described troublesome fatigue, feeling unusually cold and constipation. These symptoms have continued despite taking levothyroxine regularly. There has been no reported palpitations, tremor, unexplained weight loss, neck swelling, dysphagia or voice change. There is no history to suggest recent exposure to amiodarone or lithium. The patient reports taking levothyroxine in the morning with water, although occasionally breakfast follows within half an hour. No other regular medicines are currently reported.

On review today, the patient was alert and clinically stable. Pulse was 68 beats per minute and regular, with blood pressure 128/76 mmHg. There was no obvious goitre or cervical lymphadenopathy. The skin was mildly dry, but there was no peripheral oedema, tremor or focal neurological deficit. Cardiovascular and respiratory examinations were unremarkable. Abdominal examination was soft, with no palpable abnormality.

Recent blood tests showed TSH 8.2 mIU/L. Free T4 was at the lower end of the reference range. Thyroid peroxidase antibodies have not previously been recorded, and I would appreciate advice on whether these should now be checked alongside repeat thyroid function tests. There are no current features of myxoedema or acute clinical deterioration.

The patient has been counselled to take levothyroxine consistently on an empty stomach, at least 30 minutes before food, and to separate it from calcium, iron and indigestion remedies. We will repeat thyroid function testing after the appropriate interval following any dose adjustment. I have advised the patient to seek urgent medical attention if marked drowsiness, chest pain, breathlessness or confusion develops.

Assessment and plan

Persistent symptoms with raised TSH on levothyroxine, most consistent with under-replacement or suboptimal absorption. I would value your review of the diagnosis, adherence and dosing schedule, and recommendations regarding further tests and titration. Please also advise whether specialist follow-up is required after the next blood results.

Yours faithfully,

Dr Tilian Tomlinson, MBBS

Nursing progress note – Respiratory Medicine

Date: 7th August 2028
Patient: P. Atherton, 43 y/o
Relative present: A. SUTHERLAND

Reviewed at 08:15. Alert and orientated, speaking in full sentences. Respirations even and unlaboured on room air; observations within the prescribed parameters. Reports increased soreness of the lower leg when standing. Erythema remains visible from the ankle towards the mid-calf, with local warmth and tenderness on palpation. No blistering or drainage noted. Skin marker line remains in place; redness has not extended beyond this on review.

Mobilising short distances with a frame and one staff member. Gait cautious owing to pain but no loss of balance. Encouraged to keep the affected leg elevated when in bed or seated. Took a light breakfast and adequate fluids; no nausea reported. Passed urine independently.

Flucloxacillin administered as prescribed. Paracetamol given for leg discomfort, with partial improvement reported after review. Warmth persists, though pain is less at rest. Cannula site clean and patent. Area inspected before and after treatment; no new skin breakdown.

Assessment: cellulitis of the lower leg, currently clinically stable. Continue to monitor for progression of erythema, increasing pain, fever, rigors, confusion or haemodynamic change. Falls risk remains increased due to painful mobility; call bell left within reach and assistance reinforced. A. SUTHERLAND updated regarding the plan with the patient’s agreement.

Plan for next shift: repeat observations and skin assessment, maintain elevation, continue prescribed antibiotics and analgesia, encourage oral intake, and escalate promptly to the medical team if the erythema crosses the marked border or observations deteriorate.

Signed: Ewan Birch, Staff Nurse

text:
Emergency Department Assessment

Patient: nirvi handley
The patient, aged 43, was reviewed in the emergency department with an abrupt episode of palpitations, central chest tightness and an intense fear of dying. Symptoms began while sitting at home and reached maximum severity within several minutes. There was associated tingling around the mouth and in both hands, with a feeling of being unable to get a satisfying breath. No collapse, pleuritic pain, haemoptysis, unilateral leg swelling or preceding infective symptoms. The episode had largely settled before arrival, although the patient remained apprehensive about recurrence.

Relevant history
No known ischaemic heart disease or thromboembolic disease reported. No recent surgery or prolonged immobility. The patient describes previous brief episodes of anxiety but no prior attendance with symptoms of this intensity. No suicidal thoughts or thoughts of harming others disclosed.

Initial observations
Alert and orientated, speaking in full sentences and not visibly distressed at rest.
Pulse 102 bpm initially, regular; respiratory rate 20/min; oxygen saturation 99% on air; temperature 36.7°C; blood pressure 120/80 mmHg.
Repeat pulse after supported breathing was 84 bpm.

Examination
Heart sounds normal with no murmur. Chest clear bilaterally with good air entry and no wheeze or crepitations. No calf tenderness or asymmetry. Abdomen soft and non-tender. Neurological examination grossly normal. During discussion, breathing became rapid with recurrence of perioral tingling; symptoms eased with coached slow exhalation.

Investigations
12-lead ECG: sinus rhythm, no acute ST-segment or T-wave changes, QTc within acceptable limits.
Capillary glucose normal. Blood tests, including full blood count, electrolytes and troponin, did not identify an acute abnormality. Chest radiograph was not indicated clinically.

Clinical impression and management
Presentation is most consistent with a panic attack with hyperventilation-related paraesthesia. There is no current evidence of acute coronary syndrome, arrhythmia, pneumothorax, pneumonia or pulmonary embolism. The patient was observed until palpitations and chest tightness had completely resolved. Breathing retraining was demonstrated, with emphasis on slower nasal inspiration and prolonged expiration. Written advice on panic symptoms and avoidance of excessive caffeine was provided. No sedative medication was required.

Disposition
Discharged home with clear return precautions for persistent or exertional chest pain, syncope, sustained palpitations, breathlessness or any new concerning symptom. Advised to arrange GP review for ongoing anxiety assessment and consideration of talking therapy. Follow-up with Queen Victoria Memorial Hospital is planned for 10 Dec 2026.

Clinician: HUSSNA TERRY
Signed electronically.

Referral: hereditary breast and ovarian cancer risk assessment

Patient: Rumena Mann
MRN: 033172629

Dear Genetics Team,

I would be grateful for assessment of Rumena Mann regarding a significant family history of breast and ovarian cancer, with consideration of predictive genetic testing. The specific question is whether the reported familial BRCA1 c.68_69delAG variant is relevant to this patient and, if so, what surveillance and risk-reducing options should be discussed.

Family history

The patient reports that their mother had breast cancer before the age of 50 and subsequently developed ovarian cancer. A maternal aunt was also treated for breast cancer, and a maternal cousin is reported to have undergone testing confirming BRCA1 c.68_69delAG. The family records are incomplete, so confirmation of the result and a formal three-generation pedigree would be helpful.

Current assessment

The patient is currently well and has no breast lump, nipple discharge, skin change or pelvic symptoms. There is understandable cancer-risk concern and a request for predictive testing. No current treatment or regular medication is reported. Examination in primary care was unremarkable, including breast and axillary examination. The patient understands that testing may have implications for relatives and is willing to attend genetic counselling.

Management to date

I have discussed that a specialist consultation is required before testing, including possible benefits, limitations, uncertain findings and the impact of results on screening and family planning. The patient has been advised to obtain the relative’s laboratory report if available. No imaging or blood test has been arranged in primary care pending specialist advice.

Requested action

Please review the pedigree, verify the reported familial variant where possible and offer pre-test counselling. I would appreciate advice on eligibility for targeted predictive testing, interim breast and ovarian risk management, and appropriate follow-up for the patient and potentially affected relatives.

Yours sincerely,

A. Church
GMC: 0010662
Royal Infirmary of Edinburgh

text:
20th January 2045

Dear Specialist Parkinsonism Service,

Re: M. Mellor  
MRN: 0762030

I would be grateful for your assessment of this young adult with suspected very-early-onset Parkinson disease. The principal question is whether the presentation represents idiopathic Parkinson disease or an alternative secondary, metabolic, toxic or genetic parkinsonian syndrome, and what further investigations and treatment adjustments you would recommend.

Symptoms began in early adulthood and have progressed gradually. The patient describes a predominantly unilateral resting tremor, with slowness when dressing, reduced dexterity and difficulty initiating movement after sitting for prolonged periods. There is also muscular rigidity affecting the same side, with increasing shoulder and neck stiffness. They report a smaller handwriting sample and occasional freezing when turning in narrow spaces, but no falls. There are no reported visual hallucinations, fluctuating confusion, or prominent autonomic symptoms. Sleep is disturbed by vivid dreams, although there is no clear history of dream enactment. Mood is understandably affected by the diagnosis, without current suicidal thoughts.

On examination at review, there was a low-amplitude resting tremor of the right hand, bilateral bradykinesia more marked on the right, and cogwheel rigidity at the right wrist and elbow. Arm swing was reduced on the right, with a mildly flexed posture but preserved postural reflexes. Speech was quiet but intelligible. Cranial nerve examination was unremarkable, and there was no cerebellar or pyramidal sign. Gait was slow with shortened steps, though the patient turned independently.

The patient is currently taking co-beneldopa, with partial benefit in slowness and tremor. There has been no dyskinesia or wearing-off pattern identified so far. Physiotherapy advice regarding regular exercise, large-amplitude movements and falls prevention has been provided. The patient has not yet had a formal movement-disorders assessment or genetic counselling.

Assessment

This is a young adult with progressive asymmetric parkinsonism and a partial response to co-beneldopa. Given the unusually early onset, idiopathic Parkinson disease remains possible but should not be assumed without a broader diagnostic review.

Plan and request

Please assess the patient in a specialist movement-disorders clinic. I would particularly value advice on MRI brain imaging, appropriate blood and metabolic testing, indications for genetic testing and counselling, and whether dopamine transporter imaging or a supervised levodopa challenge would add useful diagnostic information. Please also advise on medication titration and referral to occupational therapy, speech and language therapy, and psychological support as appropriate.

Yours faithfully,

FAZAAN MCMILLAN
Referring clinician
Altnagelvin Area Hospital

To: Clinical Genetics Service
NHS number: 0002187940

Patient: B. WONG
MRN: 02661876
Referring organisation: Ulster Hospital

Dear Clinical Genetics Team,

I would be grateful for your assessment of this patient because of recurrent migraine alongside a significant family history of similar attacks in a sibling. The specific question is whether the pattern warrants genetic counselling or testing for an inherited migraine syndrome, and whether there are features that should prompt a different neurological investigation.

The patient describes episodic unilateral headache, usually accompanied by nausea and marked photophobia. Attacks have become more disruptive despite identifying sleep deprivation and missed meals as possible triggers. There is no reported persistent weakness, sensory loss, visual loss, seizure, loss of consciousness or change in personality. The sibling reportedly experiences comparable headaches; the available family history is otherwise limited, and there is no known family diagnosis of a recognised genetic disorder.

Current treatment is sumatriptan 50 mg at onset of migraine, with naproxen used when additional analgesia is required. The patient has been advised to avoid taking acute medicines on more than a limited number of days each month and to keep a headache diary recording duration, associated symptoms, triggers and response to treatment. This has helped clarify the frequency but has not established a clear inheritance pattern.

Examination in primary care was reassuring, with no focal neurological deficit identified. There are no reported red-flag symptoms such as a sudden maximal-onset headache, persistent morning vomiting or progressive neurological deterioration. I have explained that most migraine is not caused by a single inherited gene, although the family pattern may still be relevant to counselling and risk assessment.

Please review the history, advise whether genetic testing is indicated, and recommend any further neurological assessment or management. If appropriate, I would also welcome advice on the information that should be obtained from the affected sibling before testing is considered. The patient is willing to provide a detailed three-generation family history and understands that testing may not identify a cause.

A follow-up review has been arranged for 2025-06-04 to discuss your recommendations and reassess symptom control.

Yours faithfully,

Dr Dashiel Dodd, MBBS

I have explained that most migraine is not caused by a single inherited gene, although the family pattern may still be relevant to counselling and risk assessment.

Please review the history, advise whether genetic testing is indicated, and recommend any further neurological assessment or management. If appropriate, I would also welcome advice on the information that should be obtained from the affected sibling before testing is considered. The patient is willing to provide a detailed three-generation family history and understands that testing may not identify a cause.

A follow-up review has been arranged for 2025-06-04 to discuss your recommendations and reassess symptom control.

Yours faithfully,

Dr Dashiel Dodd, MBBS

LABORATORY REPORT

Patient: PELIAH BURT
MRN: 006174793
Specimen: Midstream urine and venous blood
Clinical details: Acute flank pain, dysuria and rigors. Acute pyelonephritis suspected. Current treatment includes cefuroxime and paracetamol.
Contact detail: peliah.burt78@hotmail.com

Specimen received: Urine suitable for microscopy and culture; blood samples suitable for full blood count, inflammatory markers, renal profile and blood cultures. Clinical information indicates treatment has commenced, which may reduce culture yield.

Results

Urine microscopy:
• White cells: >100 × 10^6/L
• Red cells: 18 × 10^6/L
• Squamous epithelial cells: few
• Bacteria: numerous

Urine culture:
Significant growth of Escherichia coli, greater than 10^5 colony-forming units/mL. The isolate is susceptible to cefuroxime, co-amoxiclav, gentamicin and trimethoprim; resistant to ciprofloxacin. Extended-spectrum beta-lactamase production not detected.

Blood results:
• Haemoglobin 126 g/L
• White cell count 15.8 × 10^9/L
• Neutrophils 13.4 × 10^9/L
• Platelets 312 × 10^9/L
• C-reactive protein 86 mg/L
• Sodium 136 mmol/L
• Potassium 4.2 mmol/L
• Creatinine 94 micromol/L
• Estimated GFR reported as >60 mL/min/1.73 m²

Blood cultures:
No growth to date at the time of reporting. Final interpretation will follow completion of incubation.

Interpretive comment

The urine findings and predominant E. coli growth support a diagnosis of acute bacterial pyelonephritis in the stated clinical context. The isolate is reported susceptible to cefuroxime; antimicrobial choice, route and duration should be reviewed against clinical response, renal function and local antimicrobial guidance. Persistent rigors, vomiting, hypotension or worsening flank pain should prompt urgent clinical reassessment and consideration of hospital admission.

Please correlate with examination and imaging findings if obstruction or a complicated urinary infection is suspected. Repeat urine culture is not routinely required if symptoms resolve, but should be considered for persistent or recurrent symptoms.

Planned clinical review: 17 August 2004

Validated and reported by: Dr Hasanain Bartlett, MBBS

Neonatology outpatient review
National Insurance number: BG549511A

Patient: Manelle Bourne
Clinical age: 2 wk old
Legal guardian: Naseem
Contact: manelle.bourne91@live.co.uk

Manelle Bourne was reviewed in the neonatal clinic with the legal guardian, Naseem, following an admission for neonatal jaundice. The guardian reports that the yellow discoloration of the skin has improved since phototherapy, although the baby remains sleepy during some feeds and is taking smaller volumes than usual. There has been no fever, vomiting, abdominal distension, pale stool or dark urine. Wet nappies continue, with no concern about breathing or colour change.

Birth history records that the baby was born at 39+2 weeks' gestation. Feeding has been supported with expressed breast milk and formula top-ups as advised on discharge. The guardian is waking the baby regularly for feeds and keeping a written record of intake and wet nappies.

On examination, the baby was settled in the guardian’s arms and roused with handling. Mild facial and upper chest jaundice was present, with no jaundice noted on the limbs. The anterior fontanelle was soft and not bulging. Mucous membranes were moist, peripheral perfusion was good and there was no increased work of breathing. The abdomen was soft and non-distended. Tone and movements were appropriate for the clinical stage. There was no hepatosplenomegaly.

Assessment

Improving neonatal jaundice after phototherapy, with ongoing sleepy feeding and reduced intake but no clinical evidence of dehydration or intercurrent infection today.

Plan

Continue frequent feeds, waking for feeds if necessary, and continue the documented intake and nappy record. Feeding support was reinforced, including expressing after feeds if required. The guardian was advised to seek urgent assessment through the emergency department if the baby becomes difficult to rouse, refuses several feeds, has fewer wet nappies, develops fever, becomes markedly more yellow, or has breathing difficulty. A neonatal review has been arranged for 22 October 2020. Written feeding and jaundice advice was provided, and the guardian confirmed understanding.

Accident and Emergency Specialist Assessment

Patient: Nikaya
Report/accession ID: 008587941
Occupation: software developer
Referring healthcare organisation: Royal Victoria Hospital - Medical

Reason for assessment:
Assessment of recurrent brief episodes of positional vertigo associated with nausea and unsteadiness. The history was obtained from the patient, with additional observations from the patient’s adult child.

History and clinical findings:
The patient describes a spinning sensation brought on by turning in bed, looking upwards and rising from a lying position. Individual episodes are brief and settle spontaneously when still. There is no persistent vertigo, new hearing loss, tinnitus, otalgia, diplopia, dysarthria, facial weakness, limb weakness, sensory disturbance or loss of consciousness. Nausea occurs during the episodes, without persistent vomiting. The adult child reports that the patient has appeared cautious when walking but has not fallen.

Medication reconciliation confirms prochlorperazine 5 mg up to three times daily as needed. No regular vestibular suppressant use was reported.

On examination, the patient was alert and communicated appropriately. Gait was mildly cautious but independent. Limb power, coordination and sensation were grossly preserved. There was no spontaneous nystagmus. Brief torsional-upbeating nystagmus with reproduction of the patient’s typical vertigo was elicited on right-sided Dix–Hallpike testing. Symptoms fatigued on repeat assessment. There were no focal neurological signs. Cardiovascular observations were clinically stable, and the patient was not systemically unwell.

Impression:
The history and examination are most consistent with right posterior-canal benign paroxysmal positional vertigo. The short latency, brief duration, positional trigger and fatigable positional nystagmus support this interpretation. There are no current features to suggest a central neurological cause or acute vestibular neuritis.

Management and advice:
A right-sided Epley manoeuvre was performed, with partial immediate improvement. Written instructions were provided for cautious repetition at home if symptoms recur, provided this can be done safely. Advice was given to rise slowly, use support on stairs and avoid driving, ladders or other hazardous activity while symptomatic. Prochlorperazine may be used only for troublesome nausea, using the existing prescription; prolonged routine use was discouraged.

The patient and adult child were advised to seek urgent review via A&E for continuous vertigo, inability to walk, severe headache, new neurological symptoms, chest pain or persistent vomiting. Follow-up with the GP is recommended if symptoms remain troublesome, with vestibular physiotherapy or audiovestibular referral to be considered.

Signed: Delton ROBSON  
Clinician, Royal Victoria Hospital - Medical

text:
Dear Genetics Service,

Re: yasmin russell
MRN: 060862292

I am referring this patient to Royal Infirmary of Edinburgh for assessment of hereditary breast and ovarian cancer risk and advice regarding predictive genetic testing. They attended the accident and emergency department with significant cancer-risk concern after learning further details about their family history. There is a sibling with breast cancer at a relatively young age, and the patient reports additional breast and ovarian cancers on the same side of the family. The precise diagnoses and ages at diagnosis are not currently documented, but the pattern has prompted considerable anxiety and a request for formal risk assessment.

The patient has no personal history of breast, ovarian, pancreatic or prostate cancer and is not receiving any current treatment. They deny a breast lump, nipple discharge, skin change or persistent pelvic symptoms. Examination in A&E was reassuring, with no palpable breast or axillary abnormality identified and no acute systemic concerns. This was not felt to represent an emergency presentation, but the patient would value specialist counselling rather than making decisions about testing without a clear understanding of the implications.

The family has been advised to obtain copies of relevant pathology and genetic reports where available. One result mentioned in the family correspondence is BRCA1 c.68_69delAG, although it is not yet clear whether this was confirmed in the affected relative or whether the report relates to another family member. No genetic testing has been undertaken for the patient, and there is no current surveillance plan.

Assessment

The reported family history may meet criteria for hereditary breast and ovarian cancer assessment. The result quoted above requires verification before any predictive test is considered. The patient appears to understand that testing may have implications for relatives and future surveillance, but would benefit from formal pre-test counselling.

Plan

Please review the pedigree, clarify the familial variant and advise whether targeted predictive testing is appropriate. I would also appreciate guidance on interim breast and ovarian risk management, including any recommended surveillance while the family records are being obtained. The patient has consented to this referral.

Yours faithfully,

Dr Steliana Johns, MBBS
GMC number: 0202898
For Royal Infirmary of Edinburgh

text:
Emergency Department Assessment – 28 April 2026
NHS number: 0001580931

Patient: millisa hicks
Seen at NMP - CARE OF THE ELDERLY ROYAL SHREWSBURY HOSPITAL with her partner, who provided additional history. This 18-year-old African American male patient is pregnant at 9+4 weeks' gestation and reports persistent vomiting for several days, with inability to keep fluids or prescribed cyclizine down. She has noticed reduced urine output, marked thirst and unintentional weight loss. There is no haematemesis, abdominal pain, dysuria, vaginal bleeding or diarrhoea. No previous safeguarding concerns were identified. She has no known drug allergies.

On assessment she was alert but tired, with dry lips and tongue. Pulse was 104 bpm and blood pressure 108/68 mmHg; temperature was normal and oxygen saturations were 99% on air. Abdomen was soft and non-tender, without guarding. There was no calf tenderness or peripheral oedema. Urinalysis showed concentrated urine with ketones, but no blood, nitrites or leukocytes.

Blood tests demonstrated mild hypokalaemia and a raised urea consistent with volume depletion. Creatinine was within the local pregnancy reference range, and liver function and amylase were unremarkable. Serum beta-hCG was not required today. The presentation is most consistent with hyperemesis gravidarum causing dehydration and starvation ketosis. There are no current features of sepsis, acute abdomen or significant gastrointestinal bleeding.

Treatment and decision-making

A cannula was inserted and intravenous sodium chloride commenced, with thiamine given before ongoing dextrose-containing fluids. She received intravenous cyclizine, followed by small frequent oral sips once her nausea improved. Repeat observations showed a settling pulse, and she passed urine in the department. Potassium replacement was prescribed according to the emergency department protocol.

After discussion with the on-call early pregnancy team, admission was not felt necessary provided she could continue drinking and return promptly if symptoms recurred. She was discharged with cyclizine and written advice to take frequent fluids and bland foods as tolerated. The GP and maternity service should review her antiemetic regimen and weight loss urgently. She was advised to return for inability to retain fluids, fainting, abdominal pain, fever, reduced urine output or vaginal bleeding.

Discharge clinician: Dr Aryanna HOLDER, MBBS

Patient: Sylva Pearson
Occupation: Farmer
Employer: Hirnant Housing Association
Address: 38 Glan Ely Close, Arberth / Narberth, SA67 7AA
Contact: sylva.pearson31@gmail.com

Clinical genetics review

Reason for referral: Essential hypertension with a family history of early-onset high blood pressure. The patient reports intermittent frontal headache and light-headedness for 3 days. No syncope, visual loss, chest pain, palpitations, focal weakness or episodic sweating. No symptoms suggestive of renal disease. They are taking amlodipine and ramipril regularly and report no adverse effects.

Family history: A sibling has also been investigated for hypertension. Further details regarding age at diagnosis and any renal or endocrine disease in the family are not currently available. There is no reported consanguinity.

Assessment: Current presentation is not suggestive of a paroxysmal endocrine hypertension syndrome. The symptoms may relate to suboptimal blood pressure control, although an intercurrent headache disorder remains possible. Genetic testing is not indicated solely on the information available today; this can be reconsidered if there is marked or resistant hypertension, hypokalaemia, renal abnormality, or a clearly defined familial pattern.

Plan:
• Arrange home blood-pressure readings twice daily for 7 days and bring the record to the GP surgery.
• Continue amlodipine and ramipril pending review; do not alter doses independently.
• GP to check U&Es, urine albumin:creatinine ratio, HbA1c and lipids if not recently completed.
• Seek urgent assessment via A&E for sudden severe headache, new neurological symptoms, chest pain or breathlessness.
• Obtain the sibling’s diagnosis and relevant test results, with consent, before any further genetics appointment.
• Review in genetics if additional family information or red-flag clinical findings emerge.

Nursing progress note – General Medicine

Patient: I. Sidhu
Home address: 55 Renwick Terrace, Inverness / Inbhir Nis, IV99 1AA
Contact email: indiah.sidhu76@icloud.com
Spouse present at the bedside and involved in discussion: iyla-jane parry

The patient reports increasing local pain around the postoperative wound for 3 days, with tenderness on movement and when clothing comes into contact with the area. Purulent discharge was noted on the dressing during this shift, with surrounding erythema extending beyond the immediate wound margins. The patient denies chest pain or shortness of breath but feels generally washed out. Oral intake has been reduced; they managed tea, soup and approximately half of the evening meal. Fluids encouraged and tolerated without nausea or vomiting.

Observations remain stable, with no documented fever during this shift. Respiratory rate is within the expected range and the patient is alert, orientated and able to describe their symptoms clearly. Wound assessment was completed with consent. The area is warm and tender, with a small amount of thick yellow discharge. No active bleeding or wound dehiscence seen. Dressing was removed using an aseptic technique, the wound irrigated as prescribed, and a clean absorbent dressing applied. The patient reported that the pain eased slightly after cleansing and repositioning.

A&E Paediatric Assessment

Patient: pretty akram, a 10-year-old African-American male patient
Address: 35 Patriot Grove, Reading, RG6 1AA
History from patient and father, N. Ellis. Known sickle cell disease. Severe bilateral leg and lower back pain since overnight, with reduced oral intake and two episodes of vomiting. No chest pain, cough, breathlessness, dysuria or focal neurological symptoms. Father reports usual home analgesia has not controlled this episode. No reported fever.

Arrival: 08:15. Alert but distressed, pale, dry lips. T 37.2°C, HR 118, BP 108/66, RR 22, SpO2 98% on air. Capillary refill 3 seconds. Weight not recorded. No jaundice noted. Chest clear with good air entry; no murmur. Abdomen soft, non-tender. Diffuse tenderness over thighs and lumbar paraspinal region, no swelling or erythema. Neurology grossly intact. Peripheral pulses palpable.

Investigations: FBC: Hb 82 g/L, WCC 13.4 ×10⁹/L, platelets 468 ×10⁹/L. Reticulocytes 186 ×10⁹/L. U&E satisfactory; creatinine 41 micromol/L. CRP 9 mg/L. Urine dip: concentrated, otherwise negative. Blood cultures taken because of underlying sickle cell disease; no antibiotics indicated currently in the absence of fever or sepsis features.

Impression: Vaso-occlusive painful crisis with mild dehydration. No current evidence of acute chest syndrome or focal infection.

Treatment: Oral fluids encouraged; IV 0.9% sodium chloride commenced. IV morphine administered with monitoring, followed by reassessment and prescribed regular paracetamol. Warm packs applied. Haematology advice obtained; analgesia plan agreed.

Plan: Admit to paediatric ward for hydration, observations and analgesia. Escalate urgently for fever, hypoxia, chest symptoms or increasing sedation.

Seen and documented by ARYAM SAUNDERS, Paediatric Emergency Medicine.

text:
LABORATORY REPORT

Patient: ARMAAN WOOD
MRN: 058664426
Reporting organisation: SANT TYSILIO MEDICAL CENTRE
Specimen: Midstream urine and venous blood
Clinical details: Flank pain, dysuria and rigors for 3 days. Acute pyelonephritis suspected. Current treatment includes cefuroxime and paracetamol.

Specimen status
Urine received in a sterile container and suitable for culture. Blood samples were adequately filled and not haemolysed. Results should be interpreted alongside examination findings and antimicrobial exposure.

Urinalysis
• Leucocytes: 3+  
• Nitrite: Positive  
• Blood: 2+  
• Protein: 1+  
• Glucose: Negative

Microscopy
White cells: >100 per high-power field
Red cells: 20–30 per high-power field
Bacteria: Numerous

Urine culture
Significant growth of a Gram-negative bacillus, quantified at >10^5 colony-forming units/mL. Organism identification and susceptibility testing are in progress. A supplementary result will follow when available.

Blood results
C-reactive protein: 146 mg/L (reference interval <5 mg/L) — raised
White cell count: 15.8 ×10^9/L (reference interval 4.0–11.0 ×10^9/L) — raised
Neutrophils: 13.9 ×10^9/L (reference interval 2.0–7.5 ×10^9/L) — raised
Creatinine: 102 µmol/L (reference interval 45–90 µmol/L) — mildly raised
Estimated GFR: reported with caution in the context of acute illness.

Interpretive comment
The urine findings and inflammatory response support an upper urinary tract infection, consistent with acute pyelonephritis. Cefuroxime susceptibility should be checked when the final culture report is issued; antimicrobial therapy may require adjustment according to the result, renal function and clinical response. Persistent rigors, vomiting, hypotension, increasing pain or reduced urine output warrant urgent clinical reassessment.

Follow-up review: 7th October 2020

Validated and reported by Dr Maliha Osman, MBBS
Laboratory clinician, SANT TYSILIO MEDICAL CENTRE

Discharge summary – Cardiology assessment area
National Insurance number: ZZ 86 10 33 C

Patient: Shabazz
Date of admission/discharge: 4 Apr 2019
Responsible service: Royal Infirmary of Edinburgh

Reason for admission
Presented to A&E with worsening lower abdominal pain for 3 days, abnormal vaginal discharge and deep dyspareunia. No syncope, chest pain or urinary symptoms. A friend, AJOONI SAID, accompanied the patient and provided collateral history with consent.

Assessment and results
Haemodynamically stable throughout admission. Abdominal examination showed suprapubic and bilateral iliac fossa tenderness without guarding. Pelvic examination demonstrated mucopurulent cervical discharge and cervical motion tenderness. Urine pregnancy test was negative. FBC showed mild leukocytosis; renal and liver profiles were satisfactory. Urinalysis did not suggest a urinary tract infection. Vaginal and endocervical swabs were collected; results remain pending at discharge. Pelvic ultrasound showed no tubo-ovarian abscess or significant free fluid.

Hospital course
The presentation was assessed as pelvic inflammatory disease. Following discussion of sexual health testing, partner notification and confidentiality, treatment was commenced with ceftriaxone, doxycycline and metronidazole. Pain improved with simple analgesia and oral intake was maintained. No procedure was required.

Discharge medicines
Ceftriaxone administered in hospital.
Doxycycline to complete a 14-day course.
Metronidazole to complete a 14-day course.
Avoid alcohol while taking metronidazole and for 48 hours afterwards. Take doxycycline with plenty of water and remain upright after dosing.

Follow-up and advice
Please attend Royal Infirmary of Edinburgh sexual health service for review of pending swab results, HIV and syphilis testing, and partner management. Avoid sexual intercourse until treatment is complete, symptoms have resolved and partners have been assessed. Seek urgent medical attention for fever, vomiting, increasing pain, collapse or inability to tolerate antibiotics. The friend’s locality is recorded as Lacasaidh for contact purposes.

text:
Patient: quill mccabe
Address: 21 Maesincla, Dyffryn Ardudwy, LL44 2BE
Contact: quill.mccabe15@virginmedia.com
Occupation: Cleaner
Employer: Pen-marc Community Centre

Clinical Genetics outpatient review

Thank you for attending the genetics clinic to discuss your diagnosis of essential hypertension. You described intermittent headaches and episodes of feeling light-headed, without collapse, chest pain, palpitations or visual loss. You report taking amlodipine and ramipril as prescribed. Please continue these medicines unless your GP or another clinician advises otherwise.

Your blood pressure was above the usual clinic target today, although it improved when repeated after a period of rest. The light-headedness may relate to fluctuations in blood pressure or treatment, but persistent or worsening symptoms should be reviewed by your GP. Seek urgent help through A&E or 999 if you develop sudden severe headache, weakness on one side, difficulty speaking, chest pain or marked breathlessness.

The pattern described does not, on its own, establish a rare inherited form of hypertension. We discussed that genetic testing is most useful when there are additional clues, such as hypertension that is very difficult to control, unusual electrolyte results, kidney disease, characteristic hormonal symptoms, or a strong family pattern at unusually young ages. I have therefore not arranged a genetic test today. We will reconsider this if further clinical or family information becomes available.

Please arrange a home blood-pressure record, taking two readings morning and evening for seven days, seated and rested, and bring the results to your GP surgery. The GP should review renal function, potassium and urine albumin, and check whether the current combination provides adequate control without contributing to the light-headedness. Do not stop ramipril or amlodipine suddenly.

We will write again after the information has been reviewed. If no new concerns arise, we anticipate follow-up in about 10 weeks. Please contact the clinic through the usual NHS route if your symptoms change before then.

Clinical Genetics Team

text:
Discharge summary
National Insurance number: BG 20 04 42 B

Patient: faye bailey
MRN: 024807230
Discharging service: Royal Victoria Hospital
Date of discharge: [not supplied]

Reason for admission
Admitted under general medicine with a four-day deterioration in breathlessness, increased wheeze and purulent sputum on a background of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease. There was no history to suggest chest pain, haemoptysis or aspiration. NICCI MCMANUS, the patient’s spouse, provided additional history and can be contacted via HELEN'S BAY if required.

Assessment and hospital course
On arrival, the patient was tachypnoeic with widespread expiratory wheeze and reduced air entry bilaterally. Chest radiograph showed hyperinflation without focal consolidation or pleural effusion. Blood tests demonstrated a mild inflammatory response; renal function remained satisfactory. Viral respiratory screening was negative. The presentation was felt to represent an infective COPD exacerbation without evidence of pneumonia or acute cardiac decompensation.

Treatment comprised controlled oxygen initially, nebulised salbutamol and ipratropium, a short course of oral prednisolone and doxycycline. Oxygen was weaned before discharge, and the patient maintained acceptable saturations on room air when resting and mobilising. There was good clinical response, with less breathlessness and resolution of the purulent sputum. Physiotherapy reviewed inhaler technique and breathing control. Current observations are stable, including blood pressure 120/80 mmHg.

Discharge medicines
Continue prednisolone to complete the prescribed short course and doxycycline to complete the antibiotic course. Continue salbutamol inhaler as required, using a spacer if available. Regular COPD inhalers should otherwise be continued as previously prescribed; the GP should reconcile the full medication list at the next review. No long-term oxygen was indicated at this admission.

Condition and plan
The patient is clinically improved and fit for discharge home with spouse support. A discharge letter and medication information will be sent to the GP surgery. The GP is asked to review within one week, confirm recovery, reassess inhaler technique and consider referral for pulmonary rehabilitation and smoking-cessation support where appropriate.

Safety-net advice was given to seek urgent medical help for rapidly worsening breathlessness, inability to speak in full sentences, blue lips, confusion, chest pain or failure to improve. The patient and spouse understood the plan and agreed with discharge.

Patient: khairo davis
Clinical age: 72 y/o
Seen with spouse. 4-day worsening breathlessness, now at rest on mobilising to bathroom. Two pillows increased to three; waking overnight gasping. Bilateral ankle swelling and reduced exercise tolerance. No chest pain, fever, productive cough or haemoptysis. Reports adherence with furosemide 40 mg once daily and bisoprolol.

Admit to medical ward for IV diuresis, daily weight, U&Es and medication review. Cardiology/heart failure review requested. Follow-up arranged for 10 April 2026.

Address: 178 CARDY CLOSE, KILCOO

Reviewed during evening round. Admitted with decompensated heart failure and currently reporting worsening breathlessness on minimal exertion, orthopnoea and bilateral ankle swelling for 3 days. Resting in a supported upright position; becomes short of breath when transferring from bed to chair. Mobilising only with one staff member and walking frame. Falls risk increased due to reduced exercise tolerance and postural symptoms.

Encouraged low-salt choices and to report increased breathlessness, dizziness or chest discomfort. Ongoing fluid overload with exertional dyspnoea and peripheral oedema. No acute hypoxia at rest, but clinical status remains vulnerable. Covering medical clinician informed of persistent exertional symptoms and borderline blood pressure; review requested if observations worsen.

Genetics and heart failure teams at Royal Victoria Hospital to review ongoing management and discharge support; confirm sibling has relevant contact information and understands the plan.

Observations: respiratory rate 24/min, oxygen saturations 94% on air, pulse 88 bpm regular, blood pressure 108/68 mmHg, temperature 36.7°C. Fine bibasal crackles and pitting oedema to both ankles. No chest pain reported. Alert and orientated, speaking in full sentences at rest. Fluid intake modest this shift; taking small amounts with encouragement. Urine output increased following prescribed furosemide, although remains under review. Continues bisoprolol as prescribed.

Maintained upright positioning and supported transfer to chair. Lower limbs elevated when resting. Fluid balance chart commenced and explained to patient and sibling. Encouraged low-salt choices and to report increased breathlessness, dizziness or chest discomfort. Response to diuretic satisfactory so far, with less tightness in the ankles; remains breathless on movement.

Assessment

Ongoing fluid overload with exertional dyspnoea and peripheral oedema. No acute hypoxia at rest, but clinical status remains vulnerable. Escalation advice given to seek urgent review for breathlessness at rest, falling oxygen saturations, new chest pain or reduced urine output. Covering medical clinician informed of persistent exertional symptoms and borderline blood pressure; review requested if observations worsen.

Plan for next shift: continue four-hourly observations, strict fluid balance and daily weight when safe. Reassess respiratory effort, oedema and response to diuresis. Maintain falls precautions and assisted mobilisation. Genetics and heart failure teams at Royal Victoria Hospital to review ongoing management and discharge support; confirm sibling has relevant contact information and understands the plan.

PAEDIATRIC LABORATORY MEDICINE

Patient: Shy, 9 y/o
MRN: 0616552
Specimen: blood and stool
Clinical details: School-age child with acute vomiting, diarrhoea and reduced urine output. Legal guardian reports poor oral intake. Oral rehydration solution and supportive care at home.
Weight: 28.6 kg

Results
Haemoglobin 132 g/L (115–155)
White cell count 12.8 ×10⁹/L (4.5–13.5)
Neutrophils 9.7 ×10⁹/L (1.5–8.0) H
Platelets 356 ×10⁹/L (150–450)
CRP 18 mg/L (<5) H
Sodium 134 mmol/L (135–145) L
Potassium 3.7 mmol/L (3.5–5.0)
Urea 8.9 mmol/L (2.5–7.8) H
Creatinine 61 µmol/L (20–60) borderline H
Bicarbonate 19 mmol/L (22–29) L
Glucose 4.8 mmol/L (3.5–7.0)
Lactate 1.4 mmol/L (0.5–2.2)

Stool culture: No Salmonella, Shigella, Campylobacter or Yersinia isolated.
Norovirus RT-PCR: Detected.
Rotavirus antigen: Not detected.
Cryptosporidium antigen: Not detected.

Interpretation
Mild hyponatraemia with raised urea and low bicarbonate, consistent with gastrointestinal fluid loss and dehydration. Mild neutrophilia and CRP elevation; no biochemical evidence of hypoglycaemia or significant hypoperfusion. Norovirus detected. Antibiotics not indicated on these results.

Clinical comment
Continue frequent small volumes of oral rehydration solution; monitor urine output. Urgent clinical reassessment if unable to retain fluids, increasingly drowsy, bilious or bloody vomit/stool, or persistent oliguria. Consider repeat U&E if oral intake remains poor.

Follow-up review: 25th August 2020

Patient: janie carpenter
NHS number: 000 431 0510
DOB: 25 Jul 1950
Home address: 162 North Anderson Drive, Lochdon, PA64 6AB
Report/accession ID: 0648264715

Nursing progress note – Clinical Genetics

Assessment
Reviewed on ward round for plantar ulceration to the right forefoot. Reduced sensation on monofilament testing; patient reports minimal pain despite dressing strike-through. Small amount of serous local discharge, no offensive odour. Surrounding skin warm but not markedly erythematous. No rigors or reported fever. Capillary refill preserved. Foot elevated on pillow.

Observations
Respiratory rate 18/min, SpO2 97% on air, pulse 86 bpm, BP 132/76 mmHg, temperature 37.1°C. Alert and communicating appropriately. Blood glucose monitoring continued as prescribed; no symptomatic hypoglycaemia reported.

Mobility and intake
Mobilising short distances with supervision and off-loading footwear. Reminded not to walk barefoot. Tolerating diet and oral fluids; encouraged regular hydration. Refused shower this shift, accepted assisted wash at bedside.

Interventions and response
Wound cleansed with sterile saline, dried carefully and redressed using prescribed dressing pack. Co-amoxiclav administered as charted; no immediate adverse reaction. Patient tolerated procedure, advised to report increased pain, discharge, odour, fever or spreading redness. Pressure area care completed; heels intact.

Risks/escalation
Ongoing risk of delayed healing and further tissue injury owing to reduced sensation. No acute deterioration identified. Covering doctor informed of persistent local discharge; GMC professional ID: 0910732. Continue current antimicrobial and wound-care plan pending review. Consider tissue viability/podiatry input if wound appearance worsens.

Next shift plan
Repeat observations and inspect dressing. Maintain off-loading and diabetic foot precautions. Record wound dimensions and drainage at next dressing change. Confirm blood glucose results, medication tolerance and bowel/urine output. Follow-up planned in about 5 weeks; seek earlier clinical review for systemic symptoms or rapid local change.

Patient: puteri appleby
Home address: 64 Jamaica Street, DARKLEY
Contact: 07700 900700
Location: Clinical Genetics, NHS inpatient unit
Healthcare organisation: Royal Victoria Hospital

Nursing progress note

Presentation: Admitted with decompensated heart failure. Reports worsening breathlessness, orthopnoea and swollen ankles for 3 days. Sleeping upright; reduced exercise tolerance on mobilisation to bathroom. Spouse, B. Rushton, present for part of review and updated with patient’s consent.

Observations: Alert and orientated. Respiratory rate 24/min, oxygen saturations 94% on air, pulse 96 bpm, BP 104/68 mmHg, temperature 36.7°C. Bilateral basal crackles and pitting oedema to mid-shin. Hands warm, peripheral perfusion maintained. No chest pain reported.

Mobility/intake: Mobilises short distances with one staff member and frame; becomes visibly breathless, settles with rest. Falls risk increased due to weakness and urgency of toileting. Fluid intake modest; appetite reduced. Fluid balance commenced, urine output adequate since morning. Daily weight requested.

Interventions and response: Sat upright in chair, oxygen not required at present. Furosemide administered as prescribed; increased urine output subsequently, with some reduction in ankle tightness. Bisoprolol continued as charted. Legs supported when seated. Encouraged paced activity and use of call bell before mobilising. Skin intact over sacrum and heels.

Escalation: Covering medical team informed of persistent orthopnoea, borderline blood pressure and ongoing oedema. Plan for review of diuretic response, renal function and electrolytes. Monitor for worsening hypoxia, hypotension, chest pain or reduced urine output; urgent escalation to emergency response team if deterioration.

Next shift plan:
- Four-hourly observations and respiratory assessment.
- Strict fluid balance; repeat weight when safe.
- Continue prescribed medicines and reassess response.
- Maintain falls precautions and supervised toileting.
- Confirm review by Royal Victoria Hospital team and update B. Rushton only with patient consent.

Marked azotaemia with reduced eGFR, compatible with acute kidney injury in the reported clinical context. Mild hyperkalaemia and metabolic acidosis. text:
Paediatric Respiratory Clinic Report

Patient: O. Singh
Accompanied by mother, N. Simmonds
Contact: oluwateniayo.singh31@icloud.com

Reason for review: Recent acute asthma exacerbation with wheeze, increased work of breathing and night-time cough.

History:
This is an 11-year-old African-American female child reviewed following an episode of respiratory difficulty managed in the community. Mother reports audible wheeze and faster breathing, particularly overnight, with cough disturbing sleep. No reported choking event, stridor, rash or facial swelling. Oral intake and urine output have remained satisfactory. No fever reported today. There is no current limitation from chest pain. Attendance at nursery/school has been reduced during the illness.

Examination:
Bright and interactive, speaking in full sentences. Mild intermittent expiratory wheeze bilaterally, more evident at the lung bases, with good air entry. No focal crepitations. Respiratory effort currently settled, with no nasal flaring or subcostal recession at rest. Cardiovascular examination unremarkable. No cyanosis. Chest examination improved following salbutamol administered through a spacer under supervision.

Interpretation:
Findings are consistent with an acute asthma exacerbation, currently improving, without clinical evidence of pneumonia or impending respiratory failure. The history of nocturnal cough suggests suboptimal recent control and warrants review of trigger exposure, inhaler technique and the need for an appropriate preventer strategy if symptoms persist.

Plan:
Salbutamol inhaler to be used via spacer as previously advised for relief of wheeze. Spacer teaching completed with the child and mother; technique observed and corrected, including slow inhalation and repeat dosing as directed. Written asthma action advice provided. Seek urgent assessment via A&E/emergency department if increasing work of breathing, inability to speak or drink, marked drowsiness, blue lips, or poor response to reliever.

Mother advised to arrange GP review if night-time cough continues or reliever use increases. Respiratory clinic follow-up booked for 29 Nov 1988, in about 7 weeks. Family advised to bring all inhalers and spacer to that appointment.

text:
Patient: Kassia B.
Occupation: Physiotherapist
Employer: Abercrave Sports Club
Address: 41 Ashburton Avenue, Lampeter / Llanbedr Pont Steffan, SA48 7AA
Contact: kassia.burrows18@yahoo.co.uk

Seen in cardiology clinic following referral for worsening exertional breathlessness. Over the past week has developed increased breathlessness with wheeze and thicker yellow-green sputum. No pleuritic chest pain, syncope or new peripheral oedema. Reports using salbutamol inhaler more frequently than usual, with only temporary relief. No recent hospital admission.

On examination, speaking in full sentences. Respiratory rate mildly raised; scattered bilateral expiratory wheeze with reduced air entry at the bases. Heart sounds regular, with no clinical evidence of fluid overload. Oxygen saturations satisfactory at rest. Presentation is most consistent with an acute exacerbation of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease rather than a primary cardiac decompensation.

Assessment and plan:
Started prednisolone and doxycycline as prescribed today, and advised to continue the salbutamol inhaler as required. Inhaler technique reviewed. Encouraged fluids and smoking cessation support was offered. No change to cardiac medication at present. Arranged chest radiograph and spirometry review once recovered; blood tests to include FBC, U&Es and CRP.

Safety-netted to attend A&E if breathlessness becomes severe, develops chest pain, confusion, cyanosis or is unable to manage at home. GP review booked in 19 days, with earlier assessment if symptoms are not improving over the next 48–72 hours.

text:
Discharge summary

Patient: Pearl-Rose G.
MRN: 055668322
Responsible organisation: Ulster Hospital

Reason for admission
Presented via A&E with several hours of central chest pressure associated with diaphoresis and nausea. Initial ECG showed dynamic ST-segment depression. Serial high-sensitivity troponin rose, consistent with non-ST-elevation myocardial infarction (NSTEMI). A Model X3 cardiac monitor was used during observation.

Key results
Chest radiograph: no acute cardiopulmonary abnormality.
Echocardiogram: mildly impaired LV systolic function with regional hypokinesia; no significant valvular disease.
Coronary angiography demonstrated moderate multivessel coronary artery disease without a clear target for PCI. Cardiology advised conservative medical management.

Hospital course
Treated initially with aspirin, fondaparinux and atorvastatin. Chest discomfort settled and there were no further episodes of diaphoresis or nausea. • Medically managed non-ST-elevation myocardial infarction
• Coronary artery disease
• Mild LV systolic impairment

Discharge medicines
Aspirin 75 mg once daily, lifelong.
Clopidogrel 75 mg once daily for 12 months, unless stopped earlier by cardiology.
Atorvastatin 80 mg at night.
Bisoprolol and ramipril commenced at low dose, with GP review for titration.
Fondaparinux discontinued at discharge.

Follow-up and advice
Cardiology follow-up requested, including review of the antiplatelet duration and LV function. GP to repeat U&Es and blood pressure in 1–2 weeks and arrange lipid review. Cardiac rehabilitation referral made. Avoid driving until advised in line with current guidance. Return to A&E for recurrent or prolonged chest pain, breathlessness, syncope or marked deterioration.

Dear Paediatric Diabetes Team,
NHS number: 000 376 7257

Re: Juweyriya MAHMOOD

I am referring a 10-year-old Black male child with newly diagnosed type 1 diabetes mellitus for specialist review, education and ongoing multidisciplinary support. The specific question is whether glycaemic management and the family’s insulin-monitoring plan are currently appropriate, and whether further structured support is required.

History, provided chiefly by the child’s father, ELMO CHAPMAN: several days of marked thirst, frequent urination and noticeable weight loss, without vomiting or abdominal pain. Same-day assessment confirmed hyperglycaemia with raised capillary ketones; the child was clinically alert and haemodynamically stable, with no respiratory distress. Following paediatric assessment, insulin was commenced and the family supplied with a glucose-monitoring meter. They report good engagement but remain uncertain about carbohydrate estimation, correction doses and management of intercurrent illness.

At review today, oral intake is maintained and urine frequency has reduced. Injection sites are satisfactory. Home glucose readings have been variable, including pre-meal elevations, although there have been no reported severe hypoglycaemic episodes. The father is supervising injections and recording readings. The family understand the need to seek urgent assessment if ketones rise, oral intake falls or symptoms of ketoacidosis develop.

Please assess insulin requirements, injection technique, glucose-monitoring data and education needs, and arrange dietetic and psychological input as appropriate. A primary-care review is planned in 10 days, with follow-up booked for 10/11/2019.

Yours sincerely,

Sini Gee
GP

Patient: ZAYESHA RUSSELL

Dear patient,

I am referring you to the respiratory medicine team to assess ongoing exertional breathlessness and intermittent chest tightness, and to advise whether these symptoms are respiratory in origin or related to thyroid replacement.

You have an established history of hypothyroidism, treated with levothyroxine. Over recent months you have described reduced energy, feeling unusually cold and constipation. You also become short of breath when walking uphill, without wheeze or haemoptysis. There has been no recent hospital admission. You mentioned a mild dry cough for 3 days, but no fever.

At review, oxygen saturations were normal at rest and the chest was clear to auscultation. Heart sounds were normal, with no ankle oedema. Recent blood tests showed a mildly raised TSH with free T4 within the laboratory range; repeat thyroid function tests have been requested before changing the levothyroxine dose. A chest radiograph arranged through primary care was reported as clear. No inhaler has been started.

You asked me to update your friend, Razin, about the referral, and they are aware of the plan. You are employed by CROSSMAGLEN Secondary School. The referring practice is based in ANNSBOROUGH.

Please assess lung function, including spirometry with bronchodilator response if appropriate, and consider whether further imaging or cardiac assessment is indicated. I would be grateful for recommendations regarding the breathlessness and any interaction with thyroid control.

Yours sincerely,

Dr Tawab Ross, MBBS

Patient: Elinor Platt
NHS number: 000 789 8208
Occupation: Journalist
Employer: Mayals Secondary School
Address: 83 Heol Conwy, Hendy-Gwyn / Whitland, SA34 0AA
Contact: 07700 900128

Seen in cardiology clinic following referral for intermittent left-sided discomfort, initially described as “chest pain”. On further questioning, the pain is centred in the lower back and shoots down the posterior left leg to the calf, with intermittent tingling over the lateral foot. It is worse after prolonged sitting and on getting out of the car, and improves when walking gently. No exertional chest pressure, breathlessness, palpitations, dizziness or syncope. No bowel or bladder disturbance and no saddle numbness.

Examination: comfortable at rest. Heart sounds normal, regular pulse, chest clear. Lumbar flexion restricted by pain. Left straight-leg raise reproduces the leg symptoms at approximately 45 degrees. Mildly reduced sensation over the lateral left foot; power and reflexes otherwise preserved. No focal calf tenderness or swelling.

Assessment

Features are more consistent with left lumbar radiculopathy than cardiac ischaemia. No current cardiac indication for further testing.

Plan

Reassured regarding the cardiac assessment. Continue paracetamol as required and naproxen 500 mg twice daily with food, provided there are no renal, gastric or anticoagulation concerns; take with food and stop if indigestion or bleeding occurs. Advised to remain mobile and avoid prolonged bed rest. GP to consider physiotherapy and lumbar imaging if symptoms fail to settle. Urgent assessment advised for new weakness, urinary retention, loss of bowel control or perineal numbness.

DISCHARGE SUMMARY
NHS number: 0009821865

Patient: Mallaidh
MRN: MRN-03467987
Admitting service: General Surgery, Royal Victoria Hospital
Responsible consultant: Dr Eva-Rose Ogden, MBBS
GMC number: 0140755

Reason for admission
Presented via A&E with right lower-quadrant abdominal pain, nausea and loss of appetite for 3 days. Clinical examination and blood tests supported acute appendicitis.

Key results
FBC: raised white cell count with neutrophilia. CRP elevated. U&Es and liver function satisfactory. Urinalysis negative for infection. CT abdomen/pelvis demonstrated an inflamed appendix without abscess or perforation.

Hospital course
Initial management with intravenous fluids, analgesia and intravenous co-amoxiclav. Reviewed by the surgical team; laparoscopic appendicectomy undertaken without complication. Operative findings consistent with acute uncomplicated appendicitis. Histology pending at discharge.

Discharge medicines
Paracetamol 1 g four times daily when required for pain, maximum 4 g in 24 hours.
No antibiotics required after completion of inpatient treatment.

Condition and plan
Mobilising independently, tolerating diet and passing urine. Wounds clean and dry with laparoscopic dressings intact. Discharge home today with usual GP follow-up. Surgical outpatient review only if clinically indicated; histology result to be communicated when available.

Advice given
Keep wounds dry for 24 hours, then follow wound-care instructions. Avoid strenuous lifting until comfortable. Seek urgent medical attention for worsening abdominal pain, persistent vomiting, fever, increasing wound redness or discharge.

Completed by: Dr Eva-Rose Ogden, MBBS, consultant physician
Professional identifier: 0140755

Referral to Neonatology
National Insurance number: NT514806D

Patient: Ozlem Smyth
DOB: 9 Oct 2023
Referring clinician: ALYSS CROOK

Dear Neonatal Team,

I would be grateful for your assessment of this neonate with persistent jaundice and increasingly sleepy feeding. His father, Rickylee Lin, reports that the yellow colour was first noticed at home and that intake has been reduced for 3 days. He is waking for some feeds but tires quickly and is taking smaller volumes than usual. No vomiting has been reported. Wet nappies continue, although less frequently than expected.

On review today, he appeared icteric but rousable, with mildly reduced feeding effort. Temperature and observations were stable. There was no respiratory distress, abdominal distension or clinical evidence of dehydration. Transcutaneous bilirubin remains above the expected range for his postnatal age; serum bilirubin and blood group investigations have been sent, with results pending. He has not had fever or abnormal movements.

His father works for Kippen Secondary School, and has been able to remain with him during assessment. The family have received advice regarding regular waking for feeds and monitoring urine output. Feeding support has been commenced, with expressed milk offered after attempts at the breast; phototherapy is being considered pending the serum result.

Assessment: neonatal jaundice with suboptimal intake and sleepiness. Please assess urgently, advise on the need for phototherapy and further investigation, and support establishment of adequate feeding. We will continue close observation while awaiting your review.

Yours faithfully,

ALYSS CROOK

A&E Emergency Assessment

Patient: ayzaan whitfield
DOB: 14/07/1946
Address: 155 Mawsons Mead, Glasbury / Y Clas-ar-Wy, HR3 5AA
Emergency contact: relative details recorded separately

Presenting complaint:
Sudden onset breathlessness with right-sided pleuritic chest pain since this morning. Palpitations and reduced exercise tolerance. No collapse or haemoptysis reported.

Initial observations:
HR 118 bpm, BP 120/80 mmHg, RR 26/min, SpO₂ 89% on air, temperature 37.1°C. Alert, speaking in short sentences.

Examination:
Tachycardic, regular rhythm. Increased work of breathing; equal air entry, no focal crackles. Mild right calf tenderness without marked swelling. No raised JVP. Peripheral perfusion maintained.

Investigations:
ECG: sinus tachycardia, no ST elevation.
Chest radiograph: no focal consolidation or pneumothorax.
Bloods: FBC and renal function acceptable for anticoagulation; D-dimer elevated. High-sensitivity troponin minimally raised, repeat requested.
CT pulmonary angiogram: bilateral segmental pulmonary emboli, greater burden on the right; no CT evidence of right-heart strain.

Problem / action:
• Acute pulmonary embolism with hypoxia and tachycardia.
• Oxygen commenced via nasal cannula, improving SpO₂ to 95%.
• Apixaban started after discussion of bleeding risk and medication history.
• Haemodynamically stable; no thrombolysis indication. Medical assessment unit admission for observation and anticoagulation review.

Plan:
Continue apixaban as prescribed, oxygen wean as tolerated, repeat observations and troponin. Anticoagulation clinic/respiratory follow-up booked for 4 Aug 2035.

Seen and documented by A. Marsden.

Emergency Department Assessment – Clinical Genetics

Patient: BETSEY STUBBS
Accompanied by: partner, Remi-Rai ROPER
Referring service: Withybush General Hospital
Date: today
Documenting clinician: AILEE REED

Presenting complaint
Pruritic erythematous rash and skin irritation affecting both wrists and the lower abdomen for 3 days. Started after use of a new fragranced body product. No facial swelling, wheeze, vomiting or faintness. Partner reports no fever.

Background
Known contact sensitivity to adhesive dressings. No regular medicines. Hydrocortisone cream and cetirizine tried at home with partial relief. No recent antibiotics or new foods.

Examination
Alert, comfortable, observations within normal limits. Erythematous, mildly excoriated patches with a sharp contact distribution over volar wrists and lower abdominal skin. No vesicles, purpura, mucosal involvement or cellulitis. Chest clear; no stridor or angioedema.

Investigations
No blood tests or imaging indicated. Clinical diagnosis: allergic contact dermatitis. No features of anaphylaxis or systemic infection.

Treatment / advice
Fragranced product stopped. Continue cetirizine as previously directed and apply a thin layer of hydrocortisone cream to affected skin for a short course; avoid broken skin and face. Emollient advised. Discussed avoiding further exposure and returning urgently for breathing difficulty, facial swelling, rapidly spreading rash or fever.

Disposition
Suitable for discharge. GP review if not settling or recurrent; consider dermatology/allergy assessment through Withybush General Hospital. Follow-up booked for 2024-02-26. Discharge instructions understood by patient and partner.

Signed: AILEE REED

Clinical Genetics Outpatient Report

Patient: Lake D.
Occupation: Plumber
Employer: Seascale Voluntary Service
Address: 26 Peace Pit Lane, Hampstead, NW11 0AA
Contact: lake.dodds54@virginmedia.com

Reason for review: Assessment of inflammatory joint symptoms in the context of a possible inherited susceptibility to autoimmune disease.

History and findings:
The patient reports increased morning stiffness, painful swelling affecting the small joints of both hands and marked fatigue. The hand swelling has been present for 3 days and is limiting grip and routine activities. Current treatment is methotrexate with folic acid supplementation; naproxen is being used for symptomatic relief. No recent infection or new prescribed medication was reported. There was no clinical history provided to suggest a syndromic connective tissue disorder, intellectual disability, congenital abnormality or a characteristic monogenic inflammatory condition.

Examination today demonstrates bilateral tender, swollen metacarpophalangeal and proximal interphalangeal joints, with reduced fist closure. No rash, digital ulceration or proximal muscle weakness observed. The presentation is clinically consistent with a rheumatoid arthritis flare. The fatigue may be inflammatory or treatment-related; blood monitoring is important while taking methotrexate.

Interpretation and plan:
The current findings do not, in isolation, indicate a specific genetic diagnosis or justify clinical genetic testing. Management should be coordinated with the patient’s rheumatology team, including review of disease activity and consideration of temporary treatment adjustment. Arrange FBC, renal profile, ALT and CRP in accordance with the methotrexate monitoring pathway. Continue folic acid as prescribed and avoid additional NSAIDs without medical advice. Urgent assessment is advised for fever, rapidly progressive swelling or systemic deterioration. Genetic review can be reconsidered if a significant familial pattern or atypical systemic features emerge.

Date: 5th October 2023
NHS number: 0006063790
Patient: L. RICE   DOB: 15 Sep 2003
Relative present: sibling, Krishang

Situation/concern:
Lower-leg cellulitis with spreading erythema, local warmth and tenderness, reported for 3 days. Redness has extended beyond the pen marking since admission; skin intact, no purulent discharge. Temperature 37.8°C, pulse 96 bpm, BP stable, RR 18, SpO₂ 98% on air. Alert and orientated.

Background:

text:
Dear Respiratory Medicine Team,

Re: OLEKSANDRA FARRELL

I would be grateful for your assessment of this patient with rheumatoid arthritis flare and new exertional breathlessness. The specific question is whether there is an underlying rheumatoid lung process, including interstitial lung disease, or possible methotrexate-related pulmonary toxicity contributing to the respiratory symptoms.

There has been increasing morning stiffness, swollen hand joints and fatigue over recent weeks, alongside a dry cough and reduced exercise tolerance. No acute infective symptoms have been reported. On review, oxygen saturations were 97% on air; chest examination revealed fine bibasal end-inspiratory crackles. Hand examination showed bilateral MCP and PIP joint swelling with reduced grip.

Current treatment:
• methotrexate 15 mg once weekly
• folic acid as prescribed
• naproxen with food

The methotrexate has been continued for established rheumatoid arthritis, with routine monitoring arranged through primary care. Recent blood monitoring was satisfactory apart from a mildly raised inflammatory marker. There is no previous respiratory diagnosis documented. S. CHAN, the patient’s sibling, reports that breathlessness is now limiting usual activities.

Please advise regarding pulmonary function testing and high-resolution CT, and whether methotrexate should be withheld pending investigation. I would also appreciate guidance on coordinating respiratory and rheumatology review if interstitial lung disease is identified.

The patient is employed by THE DIAMOND Secondary School. Referring clinician: ishal sewell, WARRENPOINT.

Emergency Department Assessment
National Insurance number: BG137731D

Patient: R. Barrow
DOB: 2nd October 1985
Attended with: spouse
Referring organisation: ROYAL ALEXANDRA HOSPITAL

Presenting complaint:
Two days of frequent watery diarrhoea with intermittent vomiting and crampy central abdominal pain. Spouse reports reduced oral intake since yesterday. No blood reported in stool; no recent travel or antibiotic course documented.

Assessment:
Alert, conversing appropriately, mildly dry mucous membranes. Abdomen soft, mild diffuse lower abdominal discomfort on palpation, no guarding or rebound. Bowel sounds present. No rash. Observations stable: BP 120/80 mmHg, pulse 96, temperature 37.4°C, SpO₂ 98% on air.

Investigations:
Urinalysis: concentrated urine, otherwise unremarkable.
Bloods: electrolytes and renal function within acceptable range; inflammatory markers not significantly raised.
No indication for abdominal imaging at present.

Impression:
Likely infectious gastroenteritis with mild dehydration. No clinical evidence of acute surgical abdomen or sepsis.

Treatment/actions:
Ondansetron as required administered in the department with good effect. Oral rehydration solution commenced; tolerated small frequent sips and a light snack. Antibiotics not indicated. Stool sample advised if symptoms persist or blood develops.

Disposition:
Suitable for discharge with oral rehydration solution and ondansetron as required. GP review if not improving over the next 48 hours; return to A&E for worsening pain, inability to keep fluids down, fainting or bloody diarrhoea.

Follow-up: 08/08/2026 with ROYAL ALEXANDRA HOSPITAL
Discharging clinician: Z. Johnson

Discharge summary

Patient: Tieran
Admission date: 11th February 2023
Contact: 07700 900028

Tieran was admitted with several days of lower abdominal pain, abnormal vaginal discharge and pain during intercourse. Examination was consistent with pelvic inflammatory disease (PID). Observations remained stable, including blood pressure 120/80 mmHg. Pregnancy testing was negative. Blood tests showed a mild inflammatory response; urine and vaginal samples were sent for microbiology, with no result requiring a change to the treatment plan at discharge.

Treatment was commenced with ceftriaxone, doxycycline and metronidazole. Pain and discharge improved during admission, and there was no evidence of a tubo-ovarian abscess or other need for surgery. The patient, aged 45 years, was reviewed before leaving hospital and was clinically well, eating and drinking, and able to manage oral medicines.

Please complete the prescribed antibiotic course and avoid alcohol while taking metronidazole and for 48 hours afterwards. Avoid sexual intercourse until treatment is complete, symptoms have settled and partners have been assessed and treated. Aurora-Rose Flint, identified as the partner, should contact a sexual health service for testing and treatment; partner notification can be arranged confidentially.

Follow-up with the sexual health clinic is advised to review microbiology results, symptoms and testing for other sexually transmitted infections. Seek urgent medical help for worsening pain, fever, vomiting, fainting or heavy bleeding. A copy of this summary will be sent to the GP for ongoing care.
