Report/accession ID: 07012526
Partner present: Parneet

Presenting complaint: 3-day lower abdominal pain, worsening since yesterday. Offensive yellow vaginal discharge and deep dyspareunia. No vomiting; reports dysuria, no visible haematuria. Partner concerned and attended.

Examination: uncomfortable but not toxic. Suprapubic and bilateral iliac fossa tenderness, no guarding or rebound. Speculum: mucopurulent discharge from cervical os. Bimanual: cervical excitation and bilateral adnexal tenderness, no palpable mass.

Impression: pelvic inflammatory disease; torsion/appendicitis less likely clinically. Discussed STI testing, partner notification and abstinence until treatment completed.

Treatment: ceftriaxone IM given; doxycycline and metronidazole commenced as discharge medicines. Analgesia advised.

Disposition: clinically stable for home. GP/sexual health follow-up arranged; return for fever, vomiting, collapse or increasing pain.

text:
DISCHARGE SUMMARY

Patient: NASHRA SAJID
Date of admission/discharge: 13/05/2045
Responsible team: Respiratory Medicine
Admission diagnosis: Transient ischaemic attack (TIA)

A 56-year-old White male patient admitted following sudden left arm weakness, right facial droop and slurred speech at home. Symptoms fully resolved before assessment. Partner, Soheb Simpson, from CALEDON, witnessed the episode and confirmed no loss of consciousness or seizure activity.

Key results
• CT head: no acute haemorrhage or established infarction.
• MRI brain: no acute ischaemic lesion.
• Carotid Dopplers: no haemodynamically significant stenosis.
• ECG: sinus rhythm. Routine bloods and glucose satisfactory.

Hospital course
Observed on the medical ward with neurological observations. No recurrent focal deficit. Swallow assessment passed; mobilising independently and managing oral intake. Reviewed by consultant neurologist, who felt the presentation was most consistent with TIA. Advice given regarding vascular risk-factor modification and urgent review if symptoms recur.

Medication changes
• Aspirin 75 mg once daily, commenced.
• Atorvastatin 80 mg at night, commenced.
• Other regular medicines unchanged.

Discharge condition: Clinically stable, neurologically at baseline. Discharged home with partner.

Follow-up/actions
TIA clinic referral submitted for outpatient review and further vascular risk assessment. GP to monitor blood pressure, lipids and medication tolerance.

Patient instructions: Call 999 immediately for recurrent facial weakness, arm weakness, speech disturbance or other sudden neurological symptoms; do not drive until discussed with the relevant clinician.

Discharge summary
NHS number: 000 924 3845

Patient: Seona Gilbert
Clinical age: 14 y/o
Responsible adult: father, Sami-Ul MIRZA, locality TOBERMORE
Discharging service: ROYAL VICTORIA HOSPITAL

Admitted with approximately one day of worsening abdominal pain, initially central then localising to the right lower quadrant, associated with nausea and loss of appetite. Seen in the emergency department with localised tenderness and guarding. Haemodynamically stable; pregnancy testing not clinically indicated. Current measured weight 54.0 kg.

Blood tests showed raised inflammatory markers and neutrophilia. Ultrasound was suggestive of acute appendicitis, with no drainable collection. Following discussion with the patient and father, including assent and parental consent, proceeded to laparoscopic appendicectomy under general anaesthesia. Inflamed, non-perforated appendix removed; specimen sent for histology. No operative complications.

Received intravenous fluids, analgesia with paracetamol and intravenous co-amoxiclav peri-operatively. Pain and nausea settled post-operatively, tolerated oral fluids and diet, and mobilised independently. Passing urine; wounds clean, dry and intact with dressings in place. No fever or clinical evidence of intra-abdominal infection.

Problem list:
• Acute uncomplicated appendicitis
• Laparoscopic appendicectomy
• Post-operative pain, improved

Discharge medicines:
Paracetamol as required for pain, according to the label. No antibiotics required on discharge.

Discharged home with father in good condition. Keep wounds clean and dry; shower permitted, avoid soaking until healed. No strenuous activity or contact sport until reviewed in accordance with surgical advice. School attendance when comfortable and off regular analgesia.

Follow-up: telephone or outpatient surgical review if arranged by the operating team; histology result to be reviewed through ROYAL VICTORIA HOSPITAL. GP review if ongoing pain or wound concern. Return to A&E urgently for increasing abdominal pain, persistent vomiting, fever, abdominal distension, wound redness or discharge, or inability to keep fluids down.

Patient understood the plan and was given the opportunity to ask questions.

NURSING PROGRESS NOTE

Patient: Kalicia Muhammad
DOB: 1979-04-01
Date: 31/10/2045
Ward: Respiratory Medicine
Documenting nurse: N. Latham
Informant/contact: friend, Ajus Hope

Assessment
Postoperative wound infection to right lateral chest incision. Increasing wound erythema with small-volume purulent discharge and local pain. No rigors reported. Alert, orientated, speaking in full sentences.

Observations 08:15
T 37.8°C; HR 96; BP 128/74; RR 20; SpO₂ 95% on air. NEWS2 1.

Wound
Dressing damp with purulent staining; surrounding erythema extending approximately 2 cm from wound edge. Tender locally, no wound dehiscence noted. Swab obtained as requested, labelled and sent to microbiology. Aseptic wound irrigation completed and fresh dressing applied.

Mobility/intake
Mobilising to bathroom with supervision; steady but reports discomfort on standing. Oral intake adequate, encouraged fluids. Passed urine; bowels not opened this shift.

Treatment/response
Flucloxacillin administered as prescribed. Analgesia given with partial relief; pain reduced from 6/10 to 3/10. Tolerated wound care.

Risks/escalation
Falls precautions maintained. Wound appearance and low-grade temperature reported to the covering medical team; review requested today. Monitor for spreading erythema, fever, increased discharge or systemic deterioration.

Plan for next shift
Repeat observations and wound assessment. Continue prescribed flucloxacillin, irrigation and dressing changes. Review microbiology result when available; document pain response and escalate promptly if observations worsen.

Parkinson disease previously assessed by neurology; co-beneldopa prescribing continued in primary care. Medication adherence reported as good. Advice given regarding small sips, upright positioning and supervision with meals.

Please review for aspiration risk, respiratory muscle impairment or alternative pulmonary pathology. Consider chest radiograph, spirometry if feasible, and referral to speech and language therapy. Advice on ongoing monitoring and whether a multidisciplinary Parkinson review is indicated would be appreciated.

Planned primary care review: 9 July 2023

Kind regards,

Dr Ananth Howes, MBBS

Bloods sent: FBC, U&E, LFT, CRP, troponin and BNP; results pending. IV furosemide given as prescribed locally. Fluid balance chart and urinary output monitoring commenced.

Concern/plan: Acute decompensated heart failure, possible tachyarrhythmia contribution. Senior ED review now; consider IV rate control after renal function/electrolytes. Refer medical team for admission. Escalate urgently for worsening hypoxia, hypotension or reduced consciousness. Cardiology follow-up in about 6 weeks if clinically stable.

A&E emergency assessment

Patient: G. Li
The patient, aged 77 years, was reviewed with their adult child present.
Home address: 62 Overton Walk, Margate, CT8 8AA
Contact: germain.li31@gmail.com

Presenting complaint:
Sudden left arm weakness with facial droop and slurred speech at home. Symptoms resolved before arrival. No collapse, seizure activity or headache reported. Last known well unclear; adult child provides collateral history.

Background:
No previous similar episode documented. Taking aspirin and atorvastatin. No anticoagulant use reported.

Examination:
Alert, orientated. Speech clear at review. Face symmetrical; power 5/5 in all limbs, normal sensation. No dysmetria. Gait steady. Chest clear, heart sounds normal.
BP 120/80 mmHg. Capillary glucose normal.

Investigations:
ECG sinus rhythm. FBC, U&E, CRP and coagulation screen without acute abnormality. CT head: no haemorrhage or established infarct. Carotid imaging requested.

Impression:
Transient focal neurological deficit, clinically consistent with TIA. No persisting deficit or indication for thrombolysis.

Plan:
Discussed with stroke team. Continue aspirin and atorvastatin pending specialist review; avoid driving until assessed. Same-day TIA clinic referral arranged, with urgent vascular risk-factor review. Return immediately for recurrent weakness, facial asymmetry or speech disturbance.

Disposition:
Discharged home with adult child. Written advice provided. GP follow-up requested.

Seen and signed by V. Rowley, respiratory medicine clinician.

text:
Discharge summary

Patient: Shanita
MRN: 031 643 659
Discharging service: Royal Infirmary of Edinburgh
Clinician: Miraj Anwar

Reason for admission
Admitted from the emergency department with acute pyelonephritis causing right-sided flank pain, dysuria and rigors. Initial urine testing was strongly suggestive of urinary infection. Blood tests showed a raised inflammatory response, with stable renal function. Blood cultures remained negative.

Hospital course
Treatment was started with intravenous fluids and cefuroxime, with improvement in pain and temperature. Urine culture grew a susceptible urinary pathogen; the antibiotic was reviewed with microbiology and converted to oral treatment. No evidence of obstruction was found on renal tract imaging. You have been able to drink, pass urine and mobilise safely before discharge.

Discharge medicines
Cefuroxime tablets – complete the prescribed course, even if you feel better.
Paracetamol for pain or fever, following the directions on the dispensing label. Do not take other medicines containing paracetamol at the same time.

Please seek urgent medical advice through NHS 111, your GP surgery or A&E if rigors return, vomiting prevents you keeping tablets down, pain becomes severe, you feel faint or confused, or symptoms worsen. Contact your GP if urinary symptoms have not substantially settled after completing treatment.

Follow-up
Your GP should review the urine culture result and recovery. Please arrange this in about 3 weeks. A friend living in An t-Ollach has been updated at your request and can support you with transport and medicines.

Discharged home in a stable condition with oral antibiotics and hydration advice. Ensure regular fluids unless you have previously been given a fluid restriction.

Discharge summary – Paediatrics

Patient: Maria-Elena, 6-year-old Caucasian male patient
Address: 55 Brookvale Road, SEAFORDE
Mother/carer: Romi Rushton
Patient contact: maria-elena.cope56@btinternet.com

Admission problem
Acute asthma exacerbation with wheeze, increased work of breathing and night-time cough. History obtained from mother; no fever or choking episode. Known episodic wheeze, previously assessed by consultant respiratory physician.

Key findings
On arrival: tachypnoeic with subcostal recession and bilateral expiratory wheeze. Oxygen saturations maintained in air. No focal crackles. Chest radiograph not indicated. Viral swab negative.

Inpatient treatment / progress
Salbutamol via spacer initially at frequent intervals, then spaced to four-hourly before discharge. Three doses of oral steroid given. No oxygen requirement and no antibiotics. Work of breathing settled; eating, drinking and passing urine normally. Mother observed administration and completed spacer teaching with nursing staff.

Discharge medications
• Salbutamol inhaler: 2 puffs via spacer as needed for wheeze or breathlessness.
• Complete remaining oral steroid course as dispensed.
• Continue usual prescribed medicines.

Actions and follow-up
GP review within 2–3 days; paediatric respiratory follow-up if recurrent symptoms or frequent reliever use. Asthma action plan supplied and inhaler technique checked. Avoid smoke exposure.

Condition at discharge
Clinically improved, alert and playful, comfortable in air, wheeze minimal. Discharged home with mother.

Safety advice
Return to A&E if salbutamol is needed more often than four-hourly, breathing worsens, speech or drinking becomes difficult, or there is marked lethargy.

Referral to Endocrinology
NHS number: 0001035917

Patient: mayokun dobson
Referring organisation: Queen Elizabeth University Hospital
Report/accession ID: S25-0448362

Dear Endocrinology Team,

I would be grateful for your assessment of this patient with persistent symptoms suggestive of inadequately treated hypothyroidism despite established levothyroxine therapy. The specific question is whether the current biochemical profile reflects insufficient replacement, impaired absorption or an alternative cause for the ongoing fatigue.

They attended the accident and emergency department with several months of marked fatigue, cold intolerance and constipation. Their partner reports reduced activity and increasing difficulty concentrating, without acute confusion, chest pain or breathlessness. Examination in A&E showed a dry skin texture and mild bradycardia; there was no palpable thyroid enlargement or focal neurological deficit.

Recent blood tests showed TSH 18.6 mIU/L with free T4 9.2 pmol/L. FBC, ferritin, renal profile and liver tests were not contributory. The patient reports taking levothyroxine each morning, although timing in relation to breakfast and other medicines has been inconsistent. No recent dose change is documented. There is no history supplied of thyroid surgery or radioiodine treatment.

I have advised taking levothyroxine consistently on an empty stomach and avoiding concurrent calcium or iron preparations. Repeat thyroid function tests have been requested in 19 days, with review by the GP surgery thereafter. Please advise on dose adjustment, further investigation and whether endocrine follow-up is indicated if symptoms or biochemical abnormality persist.

Yours faithfully,

H. WHITING
GMC: 0462913
Referring clinician, Queen Elizabeth University Hospital

A&E assessment – Cardiology

Patient: KEWIN ELLISON
DOB: 2 January 1958
Date: 23 Apr 2026
History from patient and adult child. Reduced urine output, fatigue and poor oral intake for 3 days. No chest pain or breathlessness reported.

Obs: BP 102/64, HR 88, RR 18, SpO₂ 97% RA, T 36.7°C.
Alert, dry mucous membranes. Heart sounds normal, chest clear. Abdomen soft, non-tender. No peripheral oedema.

Bloods: Na 136, K 4.8, urea 18.2, creatinine 246 µmol/L, eGFR 21. Previous renal function unavailable. FBC unremarkable. ECG sinus rhythm, no acute ischaemic changes. Bladder scan 112 mL.

Impression: acute kidney injury, likely pre-renal in context of poor intake; no evidence of obstruction or acute cardiac decompensation.

Treatment: intravenous sodium chloride commenced. Medication reconciliation completed; potentially nephrotoxic and antihypertensive medicines placed on temporary medication hold pending renal review.

Discussed with E. Khatun, DORKING GENERAL HOSPITAL. Admit to medical ward for ongoing fluids, strict fluid balance and repeat U&E. Documented  23 Apr 2026.

FBC and renal profile satisfactory. CRP mildly raised. Vaginal and endocervical swabs taken; results pending at discharge. Urine NAAT for chlamydia and gonorrhoea sent. Pelvic ultrasound: no tubo-ovarian abscess or free fluid.

Reviewed in the emergency gynaecology unit at 08:15. Treated empirically for PID with ceftriaxone given intramuscularly, then commenced on doxycycline and metronidazole. Doxycycline to complete a 14-day course.

Avoid alcohol during metronidazole treatment. Analgesia as required.

Results will be reviewed by the sexual health service, with contact if treatment requires adjustment. Sexual health assessment and partner notification advised; avoid sexual intercourse until treatment is completed and partners assessed. Return to A&E for worsening pain, fever, vomiting, collapse or heavy bleeding. GP review if symptoms are not settling within 48–72 hours.

text:
Molecular Genetics Laboratory Report

Patient: B. Mcleod
Report/accession ID: 08226777
Requesting service: HEXHAM GENERAL HOSPITAL - PRESCRIBING
Specimen: Peripheral blood in EDTA; germline DNA
Test requested: Hereditary breast and ovarian cancer predisposition panel
Clinical indication: Significant family history of breast and ovarian cancer; predictive testing requested owing to concern regarding inherited cancer risk. Spouse involved in discussion with the patient. Ordering clinician not recorded on this laboratory copy.

Result

No pathogenic or likely pathogenic variant identified in the genes analysed on this panel.

The familial variant BRCA1 c.68_69delAG was specifically assessed and was not detected in the submitted specimen.

Interpretation

This result does not provide evidence that the patient carries the tested familial BRCA1 variant. It substantially reduces, but does not completely exclude, the possibility of an inherited cancer predisposition. Residual risk may reflect limitations of the assay, an alternative familial variant not included or not detectable by this method, or a non-genetic familial contribution. The result should be interpreted alongside the verified family history and any previous affected-relative results.

Clinical comment

Genetic counselling is recommended to review the pedigree, confirm the familial result where available and discuss appropriate breast and ovarian risk management. No treatment is indicated on the basis of this laboratory result alone. The patient should continue routine screening unless a specialist risk assessment advises otherwise.

Follow-up genetics review: 19/12/2018

Validated and reported by: J. Brett
Laboratory genetics clinician
Report status: Authorised; clinical correlation advised.

text:
Urgent referral to the Community Mental Health Team

Patient: Menashe Dobson
Referring organisation: Royal Infirmary of Edinburgh
Report/accession ID: 094001511

Clinical question: assessment and ongoing management of a probable major depressive episode, including review of suicide risk and suitability of psychological therapy and/or medication adjustment.

This patient attended the accident and emergency department with several weeks of persistent low mood, loss of interest in previously enjoyable activities and early-morning waking. They described reduced appetite and concentration, with marked difficulty maintaining usual daily routines. A friend provided collateral history, reporting increasing social withdrawal and reduced self-care. No immediate evidence of psychosis or manic symptoms was elicited. The patient denied current intent to harm themselves, although acknowledged intermittent thoughts that life was not worth living. A safety plan was agreed before discharge, including contact with the GP surgery, NHS 111 or emergency services if risk escalates.

Sertraline is being taken as prescribed: 50 mg once daily. There has been limited symptomatic improvement to date and nausea during the first week, now settled. Mental state examination in A&E: appropriately dressed, cooperative, tearful at times, speech normal in rate and volume, objectively depressed affect, coherent thought form and no perceptual disturbance. Insight preserved.

Please arrange a timely specialist assessment, confirm the working diagnosis, undertake a fuller risk formulation and advise on psychological intervention and medication management. GP follow-up is requested in about 6 weeks, or sooner if clinically indicated.

Yours faithfully,

C. Skinner
GMC 0546514
Referring clinician, Royal Infirmary of Edinburgh

Presenting problem:
Father reports 24 hours of unsettled behaviour, frequent small-volume wees and apparent discomfort when passing urine. Reduced feeding slightly but taking fluids. No vomiting, diarrhoea or rash. No previous urinary infection reported. Birth history: born at 39+2 weeks' gestation.

Urine sample obtained by catheter: leucocytes ++, nitrites positive, blood +. Urine sent for microscopy, culture and sensitivities. Blood tests not indicated at present; no clinical features of sepsis.

Impression:
Likely uncomplicated lower urinary tract infection. Clinically stable, tolerating oral fluids.

Treatment/action:
Nitrofurantoin commenced as per local paediatric formulary; first dose given in department. Encourage fluids. Father advised regarding fever monitoring and return precautions.

Disposition:
Discharged home with father. GP review and culture result follow-up arranged through The Royal Glamorgan Hospital. Return to A&E urgently if persistent fever, vomiting, poor intake, reduced wet nappies, lethargy or deterioration.

DISCHARGE SUMMARY – GENERAL MEDICINE
NHS number: 000 815 3770

Patient: kayin elliott
DOB: 15th February 1948
Home address: 86 Tower Way, Ballachulish, PH49 4AA
Patient contact: 07700 900595

Admission reason
Spreading erythema, warmth and tenderness of the left lower leg, with cough for 3 days. Admitted for assessment and treatment of lower-leg cellulitis; spouse involved in history and discharge planning.

Key findings
• Afebrile and haemodynamically stable on admission.
• Well-demarcated erythema from ankle to mid-calf, locally hot and tender.
• No fluctuance, crepitus or clinical evidence of abscess.
• Blood tests: mild inflammatory response; renal function suitable for oral antibiotics.
• Blood cultures negative. No evidence of DVT on clinical assessment.

Hospital course
Treated initially with intravenous flucloxacillin, with reduction in erythema and pain. Converted to oral treatment once clinically improved. Paracetamol used for analgesia. Mobilising independently; oral intake maintained. No procedure required.

Discharge medicines
• Flucloxacillin to complete the prescribed course.
• Paracetamol as needed for pain, within labelled limits.

Follow-up / actions
GP review if not clearly improving within 48 hours; routine review arranged through the surgery. Return to A&E for rapidly advancing redness, severe pain, fever, confusion or inability to mobilise. Elevate the leg when resting and keep the skin clean and dry.

Discharging clinician: Consultant physician
Professional identifier: 0003927
Condition at discharge: clinically improved and suitable for home.

Community Paediatrics Referral
National Insurance number: KN195418C

Patient: Asaph, 15 y/o
Parent: A. Phillips
Home address: 122 RIVERDALE PARK AVENUE, CULLAVILLE

Reason for referral:
Persistent atopic eczema despite regular emollient use and topical hydrocortisone. Please assess severity, optimise treatment and advise on longer-term management.

History:
Several months of dry, inflamed skin with marked itching. Sleep disturbed most nights. Flares mainly in the antecubital fossae, neck and hands. No fever or systemic symptoms. Parent reports good engagement with skin-care routine; patient increasingly self-managing and assents to referral. Confidential discussion offered separately.

Examination:
Excoriated erythematous, xerotic plaques to flexures and dorsal hands. Mild fissuring at finger webs. No spreading cellulitis, weeping or crusting. No joint symptoms.

Treatment to date:
Emollient applied liberally throughout the day and after washing. Topical hydrocortisone used during flares with partial response. No recent oral antibiotics or steroids.

Clinical question:
Could you review diagnosis and treatment potency, consider steroid-sparing therapy or dermatology input, and support education around trigger avoidance and adherence? Please advise on management of sleep disturbance and provide a written action plan.

Follow-up:
GP review in about 7 weeks, sooner if deterioration. Parent aware of referral and safety-net advice.

Referring clinician: rose-marie bains

text:
Nursing progress note
Date: 28 November 2012
Patient: tasnem reilly
DOB: 28/01/2012
Parent present: nicodem lacey

Situation: Admitted with gastroenteritis and dehydration. Parent reports vomiting and watery diarrhoea for 3 days, with fewer wet nappies since yesterday. Small-volume vomits continue after feeds.

Assessment:
Alert when roused, irritable during cares. Mucous membranes dry; tears scant. Capillary refill 3 seconds. Abdomen soft, mildly unsettled on palpation. No bilious vomit noted.
Obs: T 37.4°C, HR 148, RR 34, SpO₂ 98% in air.
Urine output reduced; one wet nappy this shift. Stool x2, watery. Oral intake poor but accepting small sips.

Interventions:
Oral rehydration solution offered 5–10 ml frequently via syringe; tolerated 40 ml in total, no vomiting for 45 minutes thereafter. Continued supportive care. Nappy weights commenced. Skin care after each stool; barrier cream applied. Parent supported with paced feeds and fluid record.

Risks/escalation:
Dehydration ongoing. Covering paediatric registrar informed of intake and urine output; continue close observation. Escalate for persistent vomiting, lethargy, absent urine or deteriorating perfusion.

Plan for night shift: Strict fluid balance, repeat observations 4-hourly, offer oral rehydration solution frequently, monitor wet nappies and stool/vomit frequency. Review need for IV fluids if oral intake remains inadequate.

Documented by arsala stacey, staff nurse.

Recurrent unilateral headache, associated nausea and photophobia. Episodes occurring intermittently; no syncope or exertional chest pain reported. Partner describes patient needing a quiet, dark room during attacks.

Pattern clinically consistent with migraine. No recent change in character or sudden maximal-onset headache. Sumatriptan used at onset with partial benefit; naproxen also taken for acute symptoms. Medication adherence and frequency of use discussed.

Examination
Comfortable at rest. Cardiovascular examination: normal heart sounds, regular pulse, no added sounds. Neurological screening examination grossly normal; no focal deficit noted in clinic.

Migraine without reported red-flag features. Cardiac examination reassuring. Consider consultant neurologist input if attacks become more frequent, disabling, or refractory to current treatment.

Continue sumatriptan as previously prescribed and naproxen with food, avoiding excessive acute-medication days. Keep a headache diary, including triggers, duration and response to treatment. Review current medicines with GP if frequency increases. Urgent assessment advised for sudden severe headache, persistent neurological symptoms, collapse or marked change in pattern.

Follow-up appointment: 13th April 2035
Patient to bring headache diary and medication list.

Discharge summary – Respiratory Medicine

Patient: B. Duncan
DOB: 1939-04-26
Reason for admission: Brief episode of left arm weakness with facial droop and slurred speech, resolving before assessment in the emergency department. No persistent neurological deficit on arrival.

Initial assessment and investigations
On review, speech was clear and facial movements symmetrical. Limb power and sensation normal. Blood pressure 120/80 mmHg. CT head showed no acute haemorrhage or established infarction. Carotid Doppler without haemodynamically significant stenosis. ECG in sinus rhythm. Routine blood tests unremarkable; cholesterol elevated.

Hospital course
Admitted for TIA assessment and observation. No recurrence of weakness, facial droop or dysphasia during admission. MRI brain did not demonstrate an acute infarct. Diagnosis discussed with the patient and their adult child, Mussie, who lives in BALLYKELLY. Stroke team advised secondary prevention and outpatient review. No indication for thrombolysis or thrombectomy, as symptoms had resolved and imaging was reassuring.

Problem list
• Transient ischaemic attack with transient arm weakness, facial droop and slurred speech
• Hypercholesterolaemia
• Vascular risk-factor management required

Discharge medicines
• Aspirin 300 mg once daily until reviewed by the stroke service, then continue as advised
• Atorvastatin 80 mg once daily

No anticoagulation started. Please seek urgent medical attention via 999 if any new facial weakness, arm or leg weakness, speech disturbance, visual loss or severe sudden headache develops.

Follow-up
Rapid-access TIA clinic appointment arranged for 8 January 2022. GP to review blood pressure, lipid profile and adherence with medication, and to support smoking, diet and exercise advice as appropriate. Patient advised not to drive until they have checked the current DVLA guidance and discussed this with their GP.

Condition at discharge: Clinically stable, fully mobile, eating and drinking, and discharged home with family support.

Referral: Diabetic Foot Ulcer Evaluation

To the appropriate podiatry and multidisciplinary wound-care service:

I am referring KENNETH NEWBRY for specialist assessment of a plantar diabetic foot ulcer with reduced protective sensation and local discharge. The specific clinical question is whether the ulcer is limited to soft tissue or whether there is deeper infection, including osteomyelitis, and whether vascular evaluation or operative debridement is indicated.

The patient has diabetes mellitus with peripheral sensory neuropathy and reports a plantar wound beneath the forefoot that has not closed with outpatient wound care. Local discharge has been present for 3 days. The patient denies fever, rigors, or new systemic symptoms. Current management consists of daily cleansing, application of a nonadherent dressing, off-loading advice, and amoxicillin-clavulanate. Adherence to dressing changes has been reported as consistent, although pressure continues to occur during ambulation.

On examination in the office, there is a full-thickness ulceration on the plantar forefoot measuring approximately 1.4 × 1.0 cm, with a fibrinous base and modest seropurulent drainage. The surrounding skin is mildly erythematous without lymphangitic streaking. There is no crepitus or fluctuance. The wound probes close to, but not definitively onto, bone. Protective sensation is diminished at multiple plantar sites on monofilament testing. Dorsalis pedis and posterior tibial pulses are palpable but reduced; capillary refill is approximately 4 seconds. No acute ischemic discoloration is present.

A recent point-of-care glucose was elevated, and glycemic control has been suboptimal by history. Plain radiographs have been requested to assess for foreign body, cortical erosion, or other osseous change. A wound culture was obtained after cleansing, although interpretation will depend on the depth and quality of the specimen. The patient has been instructed to limit weight-bearing, use the recommended off-loading device, and seek emergency care for fever, rapidly spreading erythema, increasing pain, malodor, or systemic deterioration.

Please evaluate the wound promptly, determine whether additional imaging such as MRI is warranted, and advise regarding debridement, vascular studies, antibiotic selection and duration, and definitive off-loading. Continued primary-care coordination will be provided, including monitoring of glucose control and renal function while antimicrobial therapy is in use.

Referring clinician: Z. Nesterov
Professional identifier: 062446465
Service locality: Charlotte Amalie
Referring organization: GOV JUAN F LUIS HOSPITAL & MEDICAL CTR

Sincerely,

Z. Nesterov

Emergency Department Note

Patient: Mafer Kremling, a 37-year-old Hispanic male patient
Chief complaint: Left lower leg redness and pain

HPI: Reports 2 days of increasing redness, warmth, and tenderness over the left shin. Noted mild swelling this morning. Denies trauma, drainage, numbness, chest pain, dyspnea, or prior DVT. Took acetaminophen at home with partial relief. No recent travel or surgery. Home address: 878 Franklin St, Miami, FL 33167.

Triage: T 99.8°F, HR 104, BP 120/80 mmHg, RR 18, SpO2 98% room air. Pain 5/10.

Exam: Alert, nontoxic, ambulatory. Mild tachycardia with regular rhythm. Approximately 12 x 8 cm area of blanching erythema and warmth over the anterior distal left lower leg; margins marked. Tender to palpation without fluctuance, crepitus, lymphangitic streaking, or open wound. Calf compartments soft. DP/PT pulses 2+, sensation intact. No focal joint pain. Lungs clear.

Workup: CBC without leukocytosis (WBC 9.6 K/uL), hemoglobin 13.8 g/dL. CMP unremarkable; creatinine 0.8 mg/dL. Lactate 1.2 mmol/L. Venous duplex negative for DVT. No imaging evidence of soft-tissue gas.

Assessment: Nonpurulent cellulitis of the left lower leg. No abscess, ischemia, sepsis, or DVT identified. Mild tachycardia improved after oral fluids and acetaminophen.

Treatment/Disposition: First dose dicloxacillin given in ED. Continue dicloxacillin as prescribed and acetaminophen as needed. Elevate leg, follow marked borders, and return immediately for fever, rapid spread, worsening pain, drainage, or systemic symptoms. Discharged home in stable condition. Follow-up with primary care on May 31, 2035.

Attending: Calvin Moralas, MD

DISCHARGE SUMMARY

Patient: Xeniyah N.
Encounter date: December 27th, 2019
Discharge disposition: Home

Reason for admission
27-year-old Hispanic female patient admitted with two days of worsening right flank pain, burning with urination, urinary frequency, fever, and rigors. She reported nausea without vomiting. No prior history of kidney stones was documented. Zafirah Gruszka, her emergency contact, was updated during the admission.

Admission findings
Temperature was 38.7°C with mild tachycardia. Examination showed right costovertebral angle tenderness without peritoneal signs. Urinalysis demonstrated large leukocyte esterase, positive nitrites, numerous white blood cells, and moderate blood. Initial white blood cell count was 14.8 K/µL. Serum creatinine was 0.9 mg/dL, with no evidence of acute kidney injury. Pregnancy testing was negative. Renal ultrasound showed no hydronephrosis or visible obstructing calculus.

Hospital course
The clinical picture was consistent with acute pyelonephritis. Intravenous fluids and empiric ceftriaxone were started in the ED. Blood cultures remained negative. Urine culture grew greater than 100,000 CFU/mL of a susceptible gram-negative organism; susceptibility results supported oral cefuroxime. Antibiotics were transitioned to cefuroxime after the patient remained afebrile and tolerated oral intake.

Flank pain and dysuria improved substantially, and rigors resolved. Acetaminophen was used as needed for fever and discomfort. At 08:15 on the morning of discharge, she was awake, ambulatory, tolerating meals, and voiding without difficulty. Repeat leukocytosis had improved to 9.6 K/µL, and renal function remained stable.

Discharge medications
• Cefuroxime 500 mg by mouth twice daily to complete a 10-day total antibiotic course.
• Acetaminophen 650 mg by mouth every 6 hours as needed for pain or fever; do not exceed 3,000 mg in 24 hours unless otherwise directed.

Condition at discharge
Hemodynamically stable, afebrile, with markedly improved flank pain and urinary symptoms. No supplemental oxygen or indwelling device required.

Follow-up and instructions
Follow up with primary care within 3–5 days for symptom review and urine culture follow-up. Maintain hydration and complete all cefuroxime doses, even if feeling better. Return to the ED for recurrent rigors, persistent fever, worsening flank pain, vomiting or inability to take medication, confusion, fainting, or decreased urine output.

The patient’s preferred contact detail for routine follow-up is xeniyah.nelums49@aol.com.

Patient: woods haaland
Referral reason: Evaluation and management of a neuropathic plantar diabetic foot ulcer

To the diabetic foot specialist,

I am referring woods haaland for assessment of a persistent ulcer beneath the left first metatarsal head. The specific question is whether the wound requires sharp debridement, off-loading intervention, vascular evaluation, or advanced wound therapy, and whether there is any indication for imaging or treatment of osteomyelitis.

woods haaland has diabetes mellitus with reduced protective sensation in both feet. The ulcer was first noticed after a callus opened during routine activity. Current symptoms are limited to local drainage and reduced sensation; there is no significant wound pain. Drainage has been intermittent and clear to yellow/serous. The patient denies fever, chills, malaise, or new hyperglycemia. There is no spreading erythema, fluctuance, crepitus, foul odor, or visible exposed bone.

On examination in the primary care office, the plantar wound measured approximately 1.2 × 0.8 cm with a shallow clean base and surrounding callus. There was a small amount of serous discharge without purulence. The foot was warm, with palpable dorsalis pedis and posterior tibial pulses, and capillary refill was less than 3 seconds. Sensation to monofilament was diminished at multiple plantar sites. No lymphangitic streaking or proximal tenderness was present. I did not appreciate a deep sinus tract or probe-to-bone finding.

Recent diabetes control remains suboptimal; HbA1c 8.7%. Current management includes daily cleansing, a nonadherent dressing, and instructions to avoid barefoot walking. The patient has been using a removable off-loading shoe but reports inconsistent use at work with Beulah Community College. I reviewed the importance of keeping pressure off the ulcer and checking the feet every day. CANAN SAMBLANET helps with dressing changes and has been asked to monitor for fever, increased redness, swelling, odor, or purulent drainage.

Amoxicillin-clavulanate is not being continued because the current drainage is not accompanied by clinical evidence of infection. Please reassess promptly if infection develops; systemic antibiotics should be selected only if objective infection is documented. Please send recommendations regarding debridement, off-loading, dressing frequency, need for radiographs, and follow-up interval.

Thank you for evaluating this patient.

Sincerely,

Ananya Shirani
Primary care clinician
Horace

Clinical indication: Reduced urine output, fatigue, and poor oral intake for 3 days. Evaluation of suspected acute kidney injury.

RESULTS

Basic metabolic panel:
Sodium: 136 mmol/L (reference range 135–145 mmol/L)
Potassium: 4.8 mmol/L (reference range 3.5–5.1 mmol/L)
Chloride: 103 mmol/L (reference range 98–107 mmol/L)
Carbon dioxide: 19 mmol/L (reference range 22–29 mmol/L)
Blood urea nitrogen: 48 mg/dL (reference range 7–20 mg/dL)
Creatinine: 2.36 mg/dL (reference range 0.60–1.30 mg/dL)
Estimated GFR: 29 mL/min/1.73 m² (reference: ≥60 mL/min/1.73 m²)
Glucose: 96 mg/dL (reference range 70–99 mg/dL)
Calcium: 8.7 mg/dL (reference range 8.6–10.3 mg/dL)

Complete blood count:
White blood cell count: 8.7 x10^3/µL (reference range 4.0–10.5 x10^3/µL)
Hemoglobin: 13.1 g/dL (reference range 12.0–16.0 g/dL)
Platelet count: 254 x10^3/µL (reference range 150–400 x10^3/µL)

Urinalysis:
Appearance: Concentrated, yellow
Specific gravity: 1.025 (reference range 1.005–1.030)
Protein: Trace
Blood: Negative
Leukocyte esterase: Negative
Nitrite: Negative
Urine sediment: 0–2 RBCs/hpf; 0–2 WBCs/hpf; occasional hyaline casts

Urine chemistry:
Urine sodium: 18 mmol/L
Fractional excretion of sodium: 0.4%

Elevated blood urea nitrogen and creatinine with reduced estimated GFR are consistent with acute kidney injury in the current clinical context. Concentrated urine, low urine sodium, and fractional excretion of sodium below 1% support a renal hypoperfusion/prerenal pattern, likely related to poor oral intake and reduced effective circulating volume. No substantial hematuria, pyuria, or active urinary sediment is identified to suggest glomerulonephritis or acute interstitial nephritis. Mild metabolic acidosis is present; potassium is currently within the reference interval.

CLINICAL COMMENT

Correlation with prior renal function results is recommended to establish acuity and baseline. Continued monitoring of urine output, serum creatinine, electrolytes, and acid-base status is advised. The reported treatment includes intravenous sodium chloride and a temporary medication hold; medication reconciliation should specifically assess nephrotoxic agents and drugs that may worsen renal perfusion. Renal ultrasound should be considered if oliguria persists or if obstruction is clinically suspected. Urgent clinical reassessment is warranted for worsening oliguria, dyspnea, confusion, hyperkalemia, or progressive acidosis.

Referral Consultation: Lumbar Radiculopathy
SSN: 000799857

Dear Spine Specialist,

I am referring NAVIEE ALWANI for evaluation of persistent low back pain with right-sided radicular symptoms and paresthesia. The specific clinical question is whether advanced imaging, electrodiagnostic testing, or an interventional treatment would be appropriate given ongoing symptoms despite initial conservative management.

NAVIEE ALWANI reports that the pain began gradually after lifting classroom supplies and has continued for approximately six weeks. The discomfort is centered in the lower lumbar region and travels through the right buttock and posterior thigh toward the lateral calf. Intermittent tingling is reported in the same distribution. The patient also describes a separate flare of muscle tightness for 3 days, but denies new trauma, fever, unexplained weight loss, saddle anesthesia, or bowel or bladder incontinence. Sleep is disrupted when lying flat, and prolonged sitting or stair climbing increases the leg pain.

The patient works as an elementary school teacher for Wyoming Community College. Occupation: elementary school teacher. Home address: 647 S Scenic Rd, Charlevoix, MI 49720.

On examination in the office, gait was mildly antalgic, with reduced lumbar flexion and right paraspinal tenderness. Straight-leg raise reproduced posterior thigh pain at approximately 45 degrees on the right and was negative on the left. Strength was 5/5 at the hips, knees, and ankles, including dorsiflexion and great-toe extension. Sensation was slightly reduced to light touch along the right lateral calf compared with the left. Patellar reflexes were symmetric, and the Achilles reflex was diminished on the right. Distal pulses were intact. There were no clinical findings to suggest cauda equina syndrome.

Lumbar spine radiographs obtained in the office showed mild degenerative disc-space narrowing at L4-L5 and L5-S1 without acute fracture or significant spondylolisthesis. The patient has been using naproxen with food and acetaminophen as needed, with partial relief. A home program emphasizing hamstring stretching, core stabilization, and avoidance of heavy lifting has been followed for about four weeks. No epidural injection, formal physical therapy course, or prior spine surgery has been performed.

Assessment

The presentation is most consistent with lumbar radiculopathy, likely involving the right L5 or S1 distribution. Motor function remains preserved, but persistent sensory symptoms and the diminished right Achilles reflex warrant specialist assessment.

Plan and requested action

Please evaluate the patient and advise whether lumbar MRI, formal physical therapy, medication adjustment, or an epidural steroid injection is indicated. Please also comment on activity restrictions and criteria for urgent reassessment if weakness or bowel or bladder symptoms develop.

Sincerely,

Woodmael Klevgard
Referring Clinician, Primary Care

LABORATORY MEDICINE REPORT
SSN: 000 19 8599

Patient: MALORIE HARSIN
Age: 69 y/o
Collection/report date: 2035-12-29
Report/accession ID: 09055952

Clinical indication:
Painless cervical and mediastinal lymphadenopathy with drenching night sweats and unintentional weight loss. The clinical diagnosis under evaluation is Hodgkin lymphoma. The patient is receiving supportive care pending tissue diagnosis; no antineoplastic therapy is reported at the time of collection.

Specimen:
Peripheral venous blood collected in EDTA and serum separator tubes. Specimens received within stability limits and processed according to laboratory protocol.

Hematology:
White blood cell count: 12.8 x10^3/µL (reference range 4.0-10.5 x10^3/µL)
Hemoglobin: 10.9 g/dL (reference range 12.0-16.0 g/dL)
Hematocrit: 33.6% (reference range 36.0-46.0%)
Mean corpuscular volume: 84.2 fL (reference range 80.0-100.0 fL)
Platelet count: 468 x10^3/µL (reference range 150-400 x10^3/µL)
Absolute neutrophil count: 9.6 x10^3/µL (reference range 1.8-7.5 x10^3/µL)
Absolute lymphocyte count: 1.7 x10^3/µL (reference range 1.0-4.0 x10^3/µL)
Erythrocyte sedimentation rate: 72 mm/hr (reference range 0-20 mm/hr)

Chemistry and inflammatory markers:
Lactate dehydrogenase: 312 U/L (reference range 120-246 U/L)
C-reactive protein: 8.6 mg/dL (reference range <0.5 mg/dL)
Albumin: 3.1 g/dL (reference range 3.5-5.0 g/dL)
Creatinine: 0.8 mg/dL (reference range 0.6-1.2 mg/dL)
Aspartate aminotransferase: 22 U/L (reference range 10-40 U/L)
Alanine aminotransferase: 19 U/L (reference range 7-56 U/L)
Total bilirubin: 0.6 mg/dL (reference range 0.2-1.2 mg/dL)

Peripheral blood smear:
Mild normocytic anemia, neutrophilic leukocytosis, and thrombocytosis. Occasional reactive lymphocytes are present. No circulating blasts or definite abnormal large lymphoid population is identified.

Interpretation:
The findings demonstrate an inflammatory pattern with normocytic anemia, neutrophilia, thrombocytosis, elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate, elevated C-reactive protein, increased lactate dehydrogenase, and mild hypoalbuminemia. These abnormalities are compatible with an active systemic lymphoproliferative process, including the reported clinical diagnosis of Hodgkin lymphoma, but are not diagnostic by themselves. Peripheral blood findings do not establish lymphoma subtype.

Excisional or core lymph-node biopsy with histopathologic evaluation and immunophenotyping is recommended for definitive diagnosis. Correlation with imaging and clinical staging studies is advised. If tissue is obtained, submission of fresh material for flow cytometry should be coordinated with the laboratory before the procedure.

ASAD GIANGIACOMO
Laboratory validating clinician

Reporting organization: OSCEOLA COMMUNITY HOSPITAL
Patient: J. Fowler
Report/accession ID: 08941974
Specimen context: Peripheral blood collected for evaluation of increased inflammatory symptoms in a patient with rheumatoid arthritis. Clinical history provided with the order notes morning stiffness, swollen hand joints, and fatigue. Current medications include methotrexate, folic acid, and naproxen.

Results

Complete blood count:
- WBC: 8.7 × 10^3/µL (reference 3.8–10.8)
- Hemoglobin: 11.8 g/dL (reference 11.7–15.5)
- Platelets: 428 × 10^3/µL (reference 140–400); high
- Absolute neutrophils: 6.1 × 10^3/µL (reference 1.5–7.8)

Inflammation and rheumatologic studies:
- C-reactive protein: 18.6 mg/L (reference <8.0); high
- Erythrocyte sedimentation rate: 46 mm/hr (reference 0–20); high
- Rheumatoid factor: 186 IU/mL (reference <14); high
- Anti-cyclic citrullinated peptide antibody: >250 U/mL (reference <20); high

Chemistry monitoring:
- AST: 22 U/L (reference 10–35)
- ALT: 19 U/L (reference 6–29)
- Creatinine: 0.82 mg/dL (reference 0.60–1.10)
- Estimated GFR: 86 mL/min/1.73 m² (reference ≥60)

Interpretation

The elevated CRP and ESR, with reactive thrombocytosis, support active systemic inflammation and are compatible with the reported rheumatoid arthritis flare. Markedly positive rheumatoid factor and anti-CCP antibody results are consistent with the established rheumatoid arthritis diagnosis but do not independently measure current disease activity. Hemoglobin is at the low end of the stated interval. Liver enzymes and renal function are within the provided monitoring ranges.

Data-quality note

A submitted specimen-date field of 04/31/2025 was rejected because that calendar date is invalid. Results were released using the verified collection record; the invalid field should not be used for clinical timing or medication decisions.

Clinical comment

The laboratory pattern supports correlation with joint examination and functional status. Methotrexate safety monitoring is acceptable on this specimen, with no current transaminase or creatinine elevation. Continued folic acid and prescribed therapy should be reviewed by the ordering clinician; treatment escalation should be based on the complete clinical assessment rather than serology alone.

A laboratory review appointment is planned for March 7, 2018.

Escalation: Covering provider updated regarding persistent pain and limited intake. No new orders at this time. Report/accession ID: 016875829.

Next shift: Continue IV hydration, pain reassessment, intake/output documentation, and frequent respiratory checks. Encourage ambulation as tolerated. Review need for hematology and pain-service follow-up.

Discharge Summary

Patient: B. Diazgomez
MRN: 050023/35
Admitting service: Emergency Department
Treating facility: MUNSON HEALTHCARE MANISTEE HOSPITAL

Reason for admission:
The patient presented to the emergency department with several days of reduced urine output, fatigue, and poor oral intake. A sibling provided additional history and reported that the patient had been drinking very little before arrival. There was no reported chest pain, dyspnea, fever, or persistent vomiting.

Key results and hospital course:
Initial laboratory testing showed an acute rise in serum creatinine from the available prior baseline, with mild elevation of blood urea nitrogen and concentrated urine. Electrolytes remained acceptable, and urinalysis did not suggest a urinary tract infection. Bladder scanning showed no significant retention. The patient received intravenous sodium chloride with gradual improvement in urine output and oral intake. Repeat renal function testing showed improvement but had not yet fully returned to baseline.

At discharge, vital signs were stable, including blood pressure of 120/80 mmHg. The patient was alert, ambulatory, and tolerating oral fluids without nausea. There was no clinical evidence of volume overload or an indication for emergent dialysis.

Medication plan:
Potentially kidney-stressing medications were held temporarily during recovery, including nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs and the patient’s usual renally active blood pressure medication. The patient was instructed not to restart held medications until renal function has been reviewed by the outpatient clinician. No new nephrotoxic medication was prescribed. Acetaminophen may be used for pain if needed, within labeled dosing limits and unless otherwise directed.

Assessment:
Acute kidney injury, most consistent with reduced effective circulating volume from poor intake. Renal function is improving after hydration, but continued outpatient monitoring is necessary.

Discharge instructions and follow-up:
Increase oral fluids as tolerated and maintain regular meals. Avoid NSAIDs and over-the-counter herbal products until cleared. Return immediately for inability to keep fluids down, worsening weakness, confusion, shortness of breath, swelling, fever, or markedly decreased urine output. Follow up with primary care within several days for repeat basic metabolic panel, medication reconciliation, and assessment of renal recovery.

Discharging clinician: cobalt kuhl, 098542102

ED Assessment
SSN: 963693467

Patient: kreece ellston
Department: Clinical Genetics / Emergency evaluation
Report/accession ID: 03925557
Contact: kreece.ellston33@comcast.net

Chief complaint: Increasing redness, drainage, and pain at postoperative wound.

History: Reports worsening wound erythema and local tenderness over the last several days, now with purulent discharge. No measured fever, chills, vomiting, dyspnea, or diffuse rash. Partner ELITE MALTES present and provides corroborating history. Surgical dressing changed at home; no wound dehiscence noted by patient. Medication list reviewed; no current antibiotic documented.

Exam: Afebrile, hemodynamically stable, nontoxic. Postoperative wound with approximately 3 cm surrounding erythema, warmth, and focal tenderness. Small amount of thick purulent drainage expressed from the superficial edge. No fluctuance, crepitus, lymphangitic streaking, or exposed deep tissue. Distal perfusion and sensation intact.

Workup: Wound culture obtained after cleansing. CBC without leukocytosis. Basic metabolic panel without clinically significant abnormality. Bedside ultrasound shows no drainable fluid collection.

Medical decision-making: Findings consistent with localized postoperative wound infection without evidence of sepsis, necrotizing infection, or deep abscess. Case reviewed with the surgical team at Sanford Clear Lake Medical Center; outpatient treatment appropriate.

Treatment/Disposition: Wound irrigation performed; sterile dressing applied. Start dicloxacillin, once daily, as directed on the discharge prescription. Return immediately for fever, spreading erythema, increasing drainage, severe pain, or weakness. Follow up with the surgical clinic in about 4 weeks, sooner for worsening symptoms. Patient and partner verbalized understanding.

Small amount of thick purulent drainage expressed from the superficial edge. No fluctuance, crepitus, lymphangitic streaking, or exposed deep tissue. Distal perfusion and sensation intact.

Workup: Wound culture obtained after cleansing. CBC without leukocytosis. Basic metabolic panel without clinically significant abnormality. Bedside ultrasound shows no drainable fluid collection.

Return immediately for fever, spreading erythema, increasing drainage, severe pain, or weakness. Follow up with the surgical clinic in about 4 weeks, sooner for worsening symptoms. Patient and partner verbalized understanding.

Patient: B. Fleurival
SSN: 994 79 6153
MRN: M8325366
Contact: bardia.fleurival98@icloud.com
Emergency contact: Evrin Eisenhardt
Date: Today

Chief Complaint: Worsening redness and pain of the lower leg.

History of Present Illness: The patient presents to the emergency department with spreading redness, local warmth, and tenderness of the left lower leg for 3 days. The patient noticed a small area of irritation near the ankle that has enlarged despite home care. There is no reported fall, puncture wound, animal bite, recent travel, or prolonged immobilization. The patient denies chest pain, shortness of breath, fever, chills, numbness, or drainage. Current medications include dicloxacillin and acetaminophen; the patient reports taking the antibiotic as prescribed but has had continued progression of the redness. Evrin Eisenhardt is listed as the emergency contact and is available by phone.

Initial Assessment: Temperature is 99.1°F, heart rate 96, blood pressure 128/76, respiratory rate 18, and oxygen saturation 98% on room air. The patient is alert, comfortable appearing, and not toxic. Examination shows a 14-cm area of blanching erythema and warmth over the anterior lower leg with mild edema and tenderness. No fluctuance, crepitus, bullae, lymphangitic streaking, or purulent drainage is present. Distal pulses, sensation, and motor function are intact. The ankle and knee have full active range of motion. The remainder of the cardiopulmonary examination is unremarkable.

Investigations: CBC shows mild leukocytosis without left shift. Basic metabolic panel is within acceptable limits. Lactate is normal. Bedside soft-tissue ultrasound demonstrates cobblestoning without a drainable fluid collection. Venous duplex ultrasound shows no evidence of deep venous thrombosis.

Medical Decision-Making: Findings are consistent with uncomplicated nonpurulent cellulitis. There is no clinical or sonographic evidence of abscess, necrotizing infection, septic arthritis, or DVT. The patient remains hemodynamically stable and is appropriate for outpatient treatment. Pulmonary Medicine at Central Carolina Hospital was contacted for documentation review because of the department assignment; no pulmonary process was identified.

Plan and Disposition: The affected leg was elevated, and the borders of erythema were marked. The patient received the scheduled dose of dicloxacillin and acetaminophen for pain. Continue dicloxacillin as prescribed, use acetaminophen as directed, and arrange prompt primary care follow-up. Return immediately for fever, rapidly advancing redness, severe pain, weakness, numbness, vomiting, or new systemic symptoms. Discharged home in stable condition with understanding of the instructions.

Patient: ATHARVA RICKENBRODE
Location: Pulmonary Medicine, HIGHLAND HOSPITAL
Contact: (312) 555-0177
Home address: 684 US Hwy 250, Ansted, WV 25812
Emergency contact/friend: A. Fineout
Date: Current shift

Assessment: Awake, alert, answers appropriately. Increased shortness of breath with bed-to-chair transfer; expiratory wheeze throughout, diminished bases. Productive cough with thick yellow-green sputum for 3 days. Denies chest pain or hemoptysis. Skin warm/dry. Mild accessory muscle use noted during ambulation.

Vitals: BP 138/78, HR 96, RR 24, SpO2 90% on room air. SpO2 improved to 94% on 2 L/min nasal cannula. No acute confusion.

Safety/escalation: Monitor for worsening work of breathing, declining oxygen saturation, fever, chest pain, or change in mentation. Covering provider notified of purulent sputum and exertional desaturation; continue current plan.

Next shift: Reassess respiratory status and oxygen need, document sputum characteristics, assist with mobility, encourage intake, and reinforce albuterol use and smoking avoidance.

LABORATORY REPORT

Patient: Sultana Pelo
DOB: 06/16/2004
Report/accession ID: 0721732844
Specimen: Peripheral blood
Clinical indication: Rheumatoid arthritis with increased morning stiffness, swollen hand joints, and fatigue; medication monitoring during suspected flare.
Ordering clinician: Not listed
Collection context: Outpatient blood draw; specimen received within stability limits.

Results
- WBC: 8.7 x10^3/µL (reference 3.8–10.8)
- Hemoglobin: 11.6 g/dL (reference 11.7–15.5)
- Platelets: 412 x10^3/µL (reference 140–400)
- Absolute neutrophils: 6.2 x10^3/µL (reference 1.5–7.8)
- Creatinine: 0.82 mg/dL (reference 0.60–1.10)
- AST: 19 U/L (reference 10–35)
- ALT: 17 U/L (reference 6–29)
- C-reactive protein: 18.4 mg/L (reference <8.0)
- Erythrocyte sedimentation rate: 38 mm/hour (reference 0–20)

Interpretation
Mild normocytic anemia and borderline thrombocytosis are present. Elevated C-reactive protein and erythrocyte sedimentation rate support active systemic inflammation in the appropriate clinical setting. Renal function and hepatic transaminases are within the stated reference intervals.

Medication context
Current therapy includes methotrexate 15 mg once weekly, folic acid, and naproxen. The blood count and liver results do not show laboratory evidence of methotrexate-related cytopenia or hepatocellular injury at this sampling.

Clinical comment
Results are compatible with an inflammatory rheumatoid arthritis flare but are not disease-specific. Correlate with joint examination, disease activity assessment, infection review, and treatment adherence. Persistent fatigue and anemia should be reassessed clinically; consider iron studies and additional evaluation if anemia continues. Repeat monitoring should follow the treating clinician’s methotrexate protocol.

Laboratory validation
Validated and electronically signed by Riccardo Acero, laboratory reporting clinician.

Recommended follow-up: Clinical review on Dec 22, 2035.

Date: 2019-02-20
SSN: 000 66 3940

Patient: Vikhyath Turnbull
Address: 721 Savana Rd, Saipan, MP 96950
Occupation: Probate Lawyer

Referral question:
Please evaluate persistent generalized anxiety symptoms despite an adequate primary care trial of sertraline and advise on medication and psychotherapy options.

Clinical history:
Vikhyath Turnbull reports nearly constant worry across finances, health, and family responsibilities, with associated muscle tension, difficulty falling asleep, and frequent nighttime awakening. Symptoms have been present most days for several months and are interfering with concentration and work performance. The patient’s adult child has noticed increased reassurance-seeking and avoidance of routine decisions. There is no reported panic-related emergency visit, manic symptom, psychosis, or substance misuse. The patient denies current suicidal or homicidal thoughts.

Current treatment:
sertraline 50 mg once daily. Adherence is consistent, with mild transient nausea at initiation that has resolved. The patient has also reduced evening caffeine and is using a regular sleep schedule. No prior formal psychotherapy is documented.

Current findings:
At today’s office assessment, the patient was cooperative and appropriately groomed. Speech was normal in rate and volume; thought process was linear. Affect was anxious but reactive. Insight and judgment were intact. No focal neurologic concerns were identified. Screening is clinically consistent with generalized anxiety disorder, without evidence today of acute safety risk.

Requested action:
Please confirm the diagnosis, assess for comorbid depression or sleep disorder, and recommend whether to continue or adjust sertraline. Guidance regarding cognitive behavioral therapy and follow-up intensity would be appreciated. Primary care will continue medication management pending your recommendations.

Referring clinician: A. Mannas

EMERGENCY DEPARTMENT CARDIOLOGY ASSESSMENT

Patient: ESA BARENDT
MRN: 00496624
Home address: 878 4th St NE, Colton, WA 99113
Contact: (617) 555-0131
History source: Patient and partner, D. Koenemann

Chief Complaint:
Progressive shortness of breath, orthopnea, and bilateral ankle swelling.

History of Present Illness:
Patient reports approximately one week of worsening exertional dyspnea with markedly reduced exercise tolerance. Now becomes winded walking across the home and has been sleeping propped upright because lying flat causes breathlessness. Bilateral ankle edema has increased despite taking prescribed furosemide. Denies chest pain, syncope, fever, productive cough, or unilateral calf pain. Reports continued metoprolol succinate use. Partner confirms increased fatigue and several pounds of perceived fluid retention, though no home weight is available.

Focused Examination:
Alert and conversant, mildly tachypneic at rest. Bibasilar crackles extend to the mid-lung fields. Regular rhythm with an audible third heart sound. Jugular venous pressure elevated. Pitting edema extends to both shins, symmetric and without overlying erythema. Abdomen is soft and nontender. No focal neurologic deficit.

Investigations:
ECG: Sinus rhythm with nonspecific ST-T abnormalities; no acute ST-elevation.
Chest radiograph: Cardiomegaly with pulmonary vascular congestion and small bilateral pleural effusions.
Laboratory testing: BNP 2,840 pg/mL. Mild worsening of renal function from the available prior result; potassium within treatment range. High-sensitivity troponin mildly elevated but stable on repeat, without ischemic symptoms. Viral respiratory testing negative.

Medical Decision-Making:
Presentation is most consistent with acute on chronic decompensated heart failure with pulmonary and peripheral volume overload. Acute coronary syndrome, pneumonia, pulmonary embolism, and significant arrhythmia are less likely based on the history, examination, ECG, imaging, and serial biomarkers. Patient requires inpatient diuresis and monitoring.

Treatment and Disposition:
Administered IV furosemide with brisk urine output and improved work of breathing. Supplemental oxygen was available but not required after initial observation. Continue telemetry, strict intake/output, daily weights, renal and electrolyte monitoring, and cardiology-directed medication reconciliation. Hold further outpatient dose changes pending inpatient assessment. Admitted to the cardiology service in stable condition.

Clinical Genetics Referral

Patient: D. Oerther
Referring clinician: Yuhan Vanasse, 093186347
Referring locality: Jane Lew

Dear Clinical Genetics Team,

I am referring D. Oerther for evaluation of a diabetic foot ulcer in the setting of marked distal sensory loss and concern for an underlying inherited neuropathy or atypical diabetes phenotype. The specific question is whether genetic assessment could clarify the cause of the peripheral neuropathy and inform ulcer prevention and counseling for the family.

The patient has a plantar ulcer beneath the first metatarsal head with surrounding callus and a small amount of local discharge for 3 days. There is reduced protective sensation in both feet on monofilament examination, with diminished vibration at the great toes. Pedal pulses are palpable bilaterally, and the foot is warm without crepitus, rapidly spreading erythema, or systemic instability. The wound does not visibly probe to bone. A recent plain radiograph showed no acute osseous abnormality. Wound culture was obtained because of the discharge; results are pending.

Current management includes off-loading, daily cleansing, nonadherent dressing changes, and close wound-care follow-up. Amoxicillin-clavulanate was started for the local inflammatory changes, with instructions to seek emergency evaluation for fever, increasing pain, spreading redness, malodor, or color change. Glycemic control has been reviewed, and the patient has been advised not to walk barefoot.

The spouse, Y. Vardakis, reports that several relatives have had longstanding numbness and recurrent balance problems, although the family history is incomplete. There is no known prior genetic diagnosis. Please review the neuropathy and diabetes history, advise whether molecular testing is appropriate, and recommend any additional examination or laboratory evaluation. Guidance regarding recurrence risk, family testing, and coordination with endocrinology, podiatry, and wound care would also be appreciated.

Thank you for your assessment.

Sincerely,

Yuhan Vanasse
Referring clinician
093186347

CLINICAL GENETICS LABORATORY REPORT
SSN: 666-05-7865

Patient: darlet tukes
Report/accession ID: 040278080
Reporting organization: DOCTORS CENTER HOSPITAL CAROLINA LLC
Ordering clinician: Not provided

Specimen and clinical context:
Peripheral blood submitted for hereditary hypertension panel analysis. The clinical history indicates essential hypertension with intermittent headache and light-headedness despite treatment with amlodipine and lisinopril. The patient reports current discomfort of 5/10. A friend contributed to the medication and symptom history. No additional family history was provided with the requisition.

Testing performed:
Next-generation sequencing with deletion/duplication analysis of genes associated with monogenic hypertension, including abnormalities involving aldosterone synthesis, renal salt handling, and catecholamine metabolism. Analytical coverage was adequate for the reportable coding regions and canonical splice junctions. This assay does not reliably detect balanced chromosomal rearrangements, deep intronic variants, low-level mosaicism, or all regulatory-region changes.

Result:
No pathogenic or likely pathogenic variant was identified in the genes analyzed.

A heterozygous variant of uncertain significance was detected in a panel gene. Because the clinical significance of this finding is unresolved, it should not be used to establish a molecular diagnosis, alter antihypertensive therapy, or guide predictive testing of relatives. Variant classification may change as additional population, functional, and clinical data become available.

Interpretation:
The negative result reduces, but does not eliminate, the possibility of a hereditary cause of hypertension. The findings are compatible with multifactorial essential hypertension, particularly when there is no strong family history of early-onset hypertension, hypokalemia, adrenal disease, or episodic catecholamine-related symptoms. Clinical correlation remains necessary. Review of blood pressure measurements, adherence, renal function, serum potassium, and secondary causes is recommended through the treating team.

No targeted testing of relatives is recommended for the uncertain finding at this time. If the phenotype changes, new family history emerges, or additional clinical details become available, genetics re-evaluation may be appropriate.

Recommended follow-up:
Genetic counseling or clinical genetics review is recommended on January 10th, 2023 to discuss the result and any updated family history. The laboratory can reassess the uncertain variant upon request when clinically justified.

Electronically validated by:
K. Wayson
Laboratory reporting clinician

Analytical coverage was adequate for the reportable coding regions and canonical splice junctions. This assay does not reliably detect balanced chromosomal rearrangements, deep intronic variants, low-level mosaicism, or all regulatory-region changes.

Result:
No pathogenic or likely pathogenic variant was identified in the genes analyzed.

A heterozygous variant of uncertain significance was detected in a panel gene. Because the clinical significance of this finding is unresolved, it should not be used to establish a molecular diagnosis, alter antihypertensive therapy, or guide predictive testing of relatives. Variant classification may change as additional population, functional, and clinical data become available.

Interpretation:
The negative result reduces, but does not eliminate, the possibility of a hereditary cause of hypertension. The findings are compatible with multifactorial essential hypertension, particularly when there is no strong family history of early-onset hypertension, hypokalemia, adrenal disease, or episodic catecholamine-related symptoms. Clinical correlation remains necessary. Review of blood pressure measurements, adherence, renal function, serum potassium, and secondary causes is recommended through the treating team.

No targeted testing of relatives is recommended for the uncertain finding at this time. If the phenotype changes, new family history emerges, or additional clinical details become available, genetics re-evaluation may be appropriate.

Recommended follow-up:
Genetic counseling or clinical genetics review is recommended on January 10th, 2023 to discuss the result and any updated family history. The laboratory can reassess the uncertain variant upon request when clinically justified.

Electronically validated by:
K. Wayson
Laboratory reporting clinician

SSN: 000434754

Patient: I. Orcholski
Service: Clinical Genetics / Cardiology
Discharge disposition: Home with adult child

Reason for admission
Presented to the ED with central chest pressure accompanied by diaphoresis and nausea. Initial electrocardiogram showed nonspecific ST-segment and T-wave abnormalities without ST elevation. Serial high-sensitivity troponins demonstrated a dynamic rise consistent with non-ST-elevation myocardial infarction.

Hospital course
The patient was monitored on telemetry and treated with aspirin, therapeutic enoxaparin, and high-intensity atorvastatin. Cardiology evaluated the patient and recommended medical management. Transthoracic echocardiogram showed mildly reduced left ventricular systolic function with no clinically significant valvular abnormality. Symptoms resolved without recurrent chest pain, significant arrhythmia, or heart failure findings. Renal function and hemoglobin remained stable during admission.

No invasive procedure was performed. The patient participated in medication counseling and was able to repeat the warning symptoms that require emergency evaluation. The adult child was present for discharge teaching and transportation planning.

Discharge medications
• aspirin 81 mg once daily
• clopidogrel 75 mg once daily; continue with aspirin for the cardiology-directed dual-antiplatelet course
• atorvastatin 80 mg nightly
• Nitroglycerin 0.4 mg sublingually for chest pain as instructed; call 911 if pain persists or recurs after the first dose

Do not stop aspirin or clopidogrel without speaking with cardiology. Avoid nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs unless specifically approved by a clinician.

Condition at discharge
Hemodynamically stable, ambulatory, tolerating diet, and free of chest discomfort or shortness of breath.

Follow-up and instructions
Arrange cardiology and primary care follow-up after discharge. Cardiac rehabilitation was recommended. Return immediately for chest pressure, dyspnea, fainting, new weakness, black stools, vomiting blood, or uncontrolled bleeding. Home address: 652 North Expy, Atlanta, GA 30303. ED Handover – Clinical Genetics

Patient: J. Seeno | 36 y/o
Home address: 229 Painesville Ravenna Rd, Tiltonsville, OH 43963
Contact: janeth.seeno27@me.com
Accompanied by spouse.

Priority 1 – Suspected acute pyelonephritis
Several hours of worsening left flank pain with dysuria, chills, and shaking rigors. Spouse reports reduced oral intake but no confusion, syncope, vomiting, or pregnancy concern. Home medications include cefuroxime and acetaminophen; exact last doses reviewed at bedside. No medication allergy documented in the available chart.

At 08:15, febrile and tachycardic on arrival; blood pressure maintained. Alert, uncomfortable, speaking in full sentences. Left costovertebral-angle tenderness and mild suprapubic tenderness. Abdomen otherwise soft, without guarding or rebound. No rash. Peripheral perfusion preserved.

Investigations
Urinalysis: positive leukocyte esterase and nitrites, moderate blood. CBC with leukocytosis and neutrophilia. Basic metabolic panel without clinically significant renal impairment. Lactate not elevated. Urine culture sent before antibiotic administration; blood cultures obtained because of rigors. CT abdomen/pelvis considered for obstruction or stone; deferred after stable examination and reassuring renal function, with reassessment precautions.

Treatment and decision-making
IV fluids, acetaminophen, and parenteral ceftriaxone given in the ED, with symptomatic improvement and no recurrent rigors. Clinical picture supports upper urinary tract infection without current shock or peritoneal findings. Continue prescribed oral cefuroxime only after medication reconciliation and discharge prescription confirmation; maintain hydration.

Disposition
Discharge appropriate if repeat vital signs remain stable and oral intake is tolerated. Follow urine culture and adjust antibiotics if indicated. Return immediately for persistent fever, worsening flank pain, vomiting, confusion, fainting, inability to urinate, or inability to take medication.

Signed by treating clinician N. Marrett.

Discharge Summary

Patient: R. Hofstatter
MRN: 031816524
Discharging clinician: P. Gabin, 095606956, attending pulmonologist
Hospital: UNIVERSITY OF VIRGINIA MEDICAL CENTER

You were evaluated in the emergency department after developing sudden breathlessness, sharp pain with breathing, and a fast heart rate. Your sibling provided additional history during the evaluation. CT pulmonary angiography showed acute pulmonary emboli in the segmental branches of the right lower lobe, without evidence of right-heart strain. Ultrasound of both legs did not show deep vein thrombosis. Troponin and BNP were normal, and your oxygen level remained stable on room air after initial observation.

You received supplemental oxygen for comfort and were monitored on cardiac telemetry. Because your blood pressure remained stable and there was no sign of heart injury or shock, clot-busting medication and a procedure to remove the clot were not needed. The attending pulmonologist reviewed the imaging and agreed that treatment with an oral blood thinner was appropriate. There was no bleeding during the stay, and your blood counts and kidney function remained acceptable for treatment.

At discharge, take apixaban exactly as prescribed: 10 mg twice daily for 7 days, then 5 mg twice daily. Do not stop apixaban without speaking with your clinician. Avoid ibuprofen, naproxen, aspirin, and other medicines that increase bleeding risk unless specifically approved. Acetaminophen may be used for pain if you have no prior restriction. Supplemental oxygen is not required at rest at discharge; use it only if separately arranged in your discharge instructions.

Arrange follow-up with primary care within 1 week and with pulmonary medicine within 2–4 weeks to review the duration of anticoagulation and evaluate possible provoking factors. Seek emergency care for worsening shortness of breath, fainting, new chest pressure, coughing or vomiting blood, severe headache, black stools, or bleeding that will not stop.

Condition at discharge: stable, ambulatory, and speaking comfortably without supplemental oxygen. Review the medication list with your pharmacist and bring it to every follow-up visit.
