Discharge Summary – Cardiology

Patient: Karaya C.
DOB: 09/22/1973
Admission date: May 17, 2025
Discharge date: May 17, 2025
Home address: 262 Purple Heart Hwy, New Castle, PA 16101
Patient contact: karaya.comolli70@outlook.com

Reason for admission:
The patient was admitted with approximately one week of worsening shortness of breath, new orthopnea, bilateral ankle edema, and reduced exercise tolerance. The spouse provided additional history and confirmed increased nighttime coughing and difficulty lying flat. There was no reported chest pain, syncope, fever, or recent dietary illness.

Key findings:
On arrival, the patient was mildly tachypneic with bibasilar crackles and symmetric pitting edema of the lower extremities. Initial blood pressure was 120/80 mmHg. Chest radiograph showed pulmonary vascular congestion with small bilateral pleural effusions. Electrocardiogram demonstrated sinus rhythm without acute ischemic changes. Laboratory testing showed elevated natriuretic peptide and mild congestive hepatopathy; renal function remained stable during treatment. Transthoracic echocardiogram demonstrated reduced left ventricular systolic function with global hypokinesis and no hemodynamically significant valvular lesion.

Hospital course:
The presentation was consistent with acute on chronic decompensated systolic heart failure. Intravenous furosemide was administered with effective diuresis and improvement in orthopnea, edema, and oxygen requirement. The patient transitioned to oral furosemide before discharge. Metoprolol succinate was continued at the prior dose after the patient remained clinically stable without symptomatic hypotension or bradycardia. Sodium restriction, daily weights, and fluid moderation were reviewed with the patient and spouse. There was no evidence of acute coronary syndrome or active infection.

Medication changes:
• Furosemide: continue oral therapy as listed on the discharge medication reconciliation; take in the morning and monitor urine output and weight.
• Metoprolol succinate: continue current regimen.
• Other home medications: resume only as listed on the final medication reconciliation.
The patient was instructed not to stop the beta blocker or diuretic without speaking with the prescribing clinician.

Condition at discharge:
Discharged home in improved and stable condition, breathing comfortably at rest and ambulating without significant dyspnea. Trace ankle edema remained. The patient and spouse demonstrated understanding of the medication plan and warning signs.

Follow-up and instructions:
Follow up with primary care within one week and cardiology within two weeks for volume assessment, renal function, electrolytes, and optimization of guideline-directed heart-failure therapy. Weigh daily under consistent conditions and call for a gain of more than two pounds in one day or five pounds over one week. Seek emergency care for severe shortness of breath, chest pain, fainting, confusion, or inability to lie flat. Avoid high-sodium foods and keep the scheduled laboratory appointment.

Discharging service: Cardiology
Document date: May 17, 2025

Emergency Department Neurology Consultation

Patient: D. Inness
MRN: 0374379
Healthcare organization: LBJ TROPICAL MEDICAL CENTER
Occupation: Clinical Pharmacist
Emergency contact: Relative listed in the registration record

Reason for consultation: Recurrent unilateral headache with nausea and photophobia.

History of present illness:
The patient presents for evaluation of a severe unilateral headache with associated nausea and photophobia. Symptoms are consistent with the patient’s prior migraine pattern, although the current episode has been more persistent than usual. The patient denies recent head trauma, fever, neck stiffness, syncope, seizure, focal weakness, sensory loss, diplopia, or speech difficulty. No exertional or thunderclap onset is reported. Oral intake has been reduced because of nausea.

Medication history includes sumatriptan and naproxen used for acute episodes. The patient reports partial relief with this regimen but has not consistently taken the medications at the earliest onset of symptoms. No additional medication changes are documented during this encounter.

Examination:
The patient is alert, cooperative, and fully oriented. Speech is fluent without aphasia or dysarthria. Pupils are symmetric and reactive; extraocular movements are intact. Facial sensation and facial activation are symmetric. Strength is antigravity and symmetric in all extremities, with no pronator drift. Sensation is grossly intact. Coordination is normal, and gait is steady. No meningismus is present. Photophobia is observed during the examination, and the patient intermittently shields the eyes from room lighting.

Assessment and interpretation:
Clinical presentation and nonfocal neurologic examination support migraine without current evidence of an acute focal neurologic complication. There are no reported red-flag features requiring emergent neuroimaging based on today’s assessment. Differential considerations include tension-type headache and medication-overuse headache; the latter should be reconsidered if acute medications are used frequently.

Plan:
Treat symptomatically in the emergency department with hydration and an antiemetic, followed by reassessment of headache intensity and oral tolerance. If symptoms improve and the examination remains stable, discharge with instructions to use sumatriptan and naproxen according to the established prescription directions and to avoid excessive acute-medication use. Return immediately for abrupt maximal headache, persistent vomiting, fever, neck stiffness, confusion, fainting, new weakness, vision loss, or difficulty speaking. Outpatient follow-up with primary care and the attending neurologist is recommended for preventive-strategy review.

Consulting clinician: RAYLON KAFLEY, attending neurologist

Disposition: Discharge home with oral cefuroxime, hydration, and acetaminophen as directed. Return for persistent vomiting, worsening pain, confusion, syncope, or fever. Primary care follow-up for culture review.

Clinical Genetics Referral

Patient: Sobhan Desormeau
Home address: 685 Revere Blvd, Bedford, PA 15522
Report/accession ID: 25/257937

Dear Clinical Genetics Team,

I am referring Sobhan Desormeau for assessment of atrial fibrillation with concern for a possible inherited arrhythmia or cardiomyopathy syndrome. The specific question is whether genetic evaluation and counseling are indicated, including guidance on testing for the patient and potentially affected relatives.

The patient reports intermittent palpitations, reduced exercise tolerance, fatigue, and exertional breathlessness. Episodes are not associated with syncope or chest pain. Atrial fibrillation was documented on a 12-lead ECG during an emergency department evaluation and has subsequently recurred on ambulatory monitoring. The tracing showed an irregularly irregular rhythm without pre-excitation. Echocardiography demonstrated preserved left ventricular systolic function and mild left atrial enlargement, without significant valvular disease. Thyroid studies and electrolytes were unrevealing. Report/accession ID 25/257937 is associated with the ambulatory monitoring result.

Current medications are apixaban and metoprolol succinate. The patient reports partial improvement in palpitations since starting metoprolol, although fatigue and breathlessness with stairs persist. There has been no bleeding complication on anticoagulation. Family history is incomplete; the patient recalls that more than one relative had an arrhythmia or sudden death at an unclear age, but available records have not yet clarified the diagnoses.

Assessment: Paroxysmal atrial fibrillation with preserved ventricular function and a potentially significant, incompletely characterized family history. The early or familial nature of the presentation cannot be established from the current records alone.

Requested action: Please review the indication for genetic counseling and testing, advise whether a cardiomyopathy or arrhythmia panel is appropriate, and recommend a family-screening strategy if a pathogenic variant is identified. Please also advise whether additional cardiac imaging or electrophysiology evaluation should be arranged.

A follow-up review is planned for January 14th, 2013. Thank you for your assessment.

Sincerely,

KYA PERIUS
attending cardiologist

Discharge Summary
SSN: 000-51-2439

Patient: Layne D.
Admission/discharge date: May 26, 2028
Service: Clinical Genetics, Hampshire Memorial Hospital

You were admitted after developing sudden breathlessness, sharp pain with breathing, and a fast heartbeat. Testing in the emergency department showed a pulmonary embolism, meaning a blood clot had traveled to the blood vessels in the lungs. CT pulmonary angiography confirmed clot burden in the right lower lobe branches. There was no evidence of right-heart strain, and the cardiac ultrasound was reassuring. Leg ultrasound did not show a deep-vein clot.

You were treated with apixaban and supplemental oxygen. Your breathing and pleuritic pain improved, and oxygen was gradually reduced. You were comfortable on room air before discharge. Kidney function and blood counts remained stable. At 08:15 on the morning of discharge, you were walking in the hallway without dizziness or worsening shortness of breath.

Discharge medications:
• Apixaban 10 mg twice daily through the evening dose on May 26, 2028, then 5 mg twice daily.
• Do not stop apixaban without speaking with your prescribing clinician. Avoid ibuprofen, naproxen, and aspirin unless specifically directed. Acetaminophen may be used for pain if safe for you.
• Supplemental oxygen is not required at discharge.

Because this clot was not clearly explained by a temporary risk factor, follow-up with hematology and primary care is recommended to review duration of anticoagulation and whether additional clotting evaluation is appropriate. The clinical genetics team at Hampshire Memorial Hospital may coordinate further review if your personal or family history suggests an inherited risk.

Please seek emergency care for severe or worsening breathlessness, fainting, chest pain that is not improving, coughing blood, or uncontrolled bleeding. Report black stools, blood in urine, unusual bruising, or a significant fall promptly. Your partner, dalina bremen from Prichard, participated in discharge teaching and received the same medication and bleeding-safety instructions.

ED HANDOVER – Acute dyspnea / volume overload
SSN: 666 87 7243

Patient: Brylan  |  84 y/o
Home address: 136 Co Hwy U W, Ettrick, WI 54627
Arrived with partner.

Priority 1 – breathing:
Progressive shortness of breath over several days, now unable to lie flat. Reports three-pillow orthopnea, bilateral ankle swelling, and markedly reduced exercise tolerance. No pleuritic pain, fever, or hemoptysis. Partner reports missed evening furosemide doses this week because of frequent urination.

Triage at 08:15: tachypneic, hypertensive, oxygen saturation 88% on room air. Improved to 95% on 2 L nasal cannula. Bibasilar crackles to mid-lung fields; pitting edema to both shins. Cardiac rhythm regular, no new murmur. Abdomen soft, nontender. Alert and speaking in short sentences.

Investigations:
ECG: sinus tachycardia with chronic-appearing left bundle branch block; no acute ST elevation. Chest x-ray demonstrates cardiomegaly and pulmonary vascular congestion with small bilateral effusions. BNP elevated. Troponin mildly elevated but flat on repeat. Creatinine above reported baseline; potassium acceptable. Viral respiratory panel negative.

Treatment/decision-making:
IV furosemide administered with urine output and work of breathing improving. Continue oxygen, telemetry, strict intake/output, daily weights. Hold additional beta-blocker escalation while acutely congested; continue metoprolol succinate if blood pressure and perfusion remain stable. Findings support acute decompensated heart failure rather than pneumonia or primary COPD flare. Admit to medicine for IV diuresis and renal/electrolyte monitoring.

Handoff to admitting team: TASFIA SCHAPPACHER. Cardiology/heart-failure review requested. Return precautions reviewed with partner. Outpatient follow-up planned for 2035-10-11.

LABORATORY REPORT – WOUND CULTURE

Patient: Brystal
MRN: 0946127
Specimen: Deep plantar ulcer swab, left foot
Clinical history: A 49-year-old Asian female patient with diabetes, plantar ulceration, reduced sensation, and local discharge for 3 days. Current treatment includes wound care and amoxicillin-clavulanate.

Specimen quality: Adequate. Gram stain with moderate polymorphonuclear leukocytes; no squamous epithelial cell excess.

Culture:
- Moderate growth: Staphylococcus aureus
- Light growth: Enterococcus faecalis
- Mixed skin flora: scant
- Anaerobic culture: No anaerobes isolated

Susceptibility:
Staphylococcus aureus: susceptible to oxacillin, clindamycin, doxycycline, and trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole; resistant to penicillin.
Enterococcus faecalis: susceptible to ampicillin and vancomycin.

Interpretation: Growth of S. aureus from this specimen is potentially clinically significant in the setting of an actively draining diabetic foot ulcer. Mixed low-level flora may reflect colonization. Correlate with depth of ulcer, surrounding erythema, systemic findings, and vascular status. Culture does not assess osteomyelitis.

Laboratory comment: Results support continued clinical assessment of response to amoxicillin-clavulanate. If worsening drainage, progressive erythema, fever, tissue necrosis, or exposed bone is present, prompt surgical/podiatric evaluation and imaging are recommended. Consider blood cultures if systemic illness develops.

Follow-up review: September 11, 2035

Validated by: rupert balbaugh
Pulmonary Medicine Laboratory/Clinical Review

Pulmonary Medicine Clinic Note

Patient: AJOONI YUSUPOVA
MRN: MRN-01223221
Date: 04/22/2004
Contact: (212) 555-0104
Clinical age: 46 y/o

Chief Concern: Low back pain with shooting pain into the left leg.

History of Present Illness:
Reports approximately 3 weeks of low lumbar pain, initially intermittent and now present most of the day. Pain travels through the left buttock and posterior thigh to the calf, with intermittent tingling in the lateral foot. Worse with prolonged sitting, bending, and getting out of a chair. No recent fall or direct injury. Denies fever, unexplained weight loss, urinary retention, urinary incontinence, saddle numbness, or progressive leg weakness. Walking remains possible but limited by pain. Acetaminophen provides partial relief. Has also been using naproxen 500 mg twice daily with food.

Medication reconciliation completed. No anticoagulant use reported.

Exam:
No acute distress, mildly guarded transitions from sitting to standing. Lumbar flexion limited by pain. Left paraspinal tenderness without midline bony tenderness. Positive straight-leg raise on the left. Strength 5/5 in bilateral hip flexion, knee extension, ankle dorsiflexion, and great-toe extension. Sensation mildly diminished subjectively along the left lateral calf; right side intact. Patellar and Achilles reflexes symmetric. Gait mildly antalgic. No respiratory complaint or abnormal pulmonary finding on focused examination.

Assessment:
Lumbar radiculopathy, likely left L5/S1 distribution. No current red-flag features or objective motor deficit.

Plan:
Continue naproxen with food; avoid additional NSAIDs. May use acetaminophen between doses within label limits. Heat, gentle activity, and avoidance of prolonged bed rest. Referral to physical therapy for core stabilization and nerve-mobility work. Consider lumbar MRI or spine referral if symptoms persist beyond conservative treatment, worsen, or weakness develops. Emergency precautions reviewed for bowel/bladder dysfunction, saddle anesthesia, or rapidly progressive weakness. Follow up with primary care in 4 weeks or sooner as needed.

DISCHARGE SUMMARY

Patient: L. Policelli
Encounter date: June 30, 2012
Home address: 286 S Mecklenburg Ave, Walkerton, VA 23177
Contact: ladarrius.policelli63@hotmail.com

Reason for admission: 76-year-old South Asian male patient admitted with increasing erythema, purulent drainage, and localized pain at the postoperative wound. Symptoms present for 3 days. No chest pain, dyspnea, or systemic instability reported.

Hospital course: Wound evaluated by the surgical service. Bedside opening of a small superficial area performed; scant purulence expressed. Wound irrigated thoroughly and dressed. No evidence of fascial disruption or deep space infection on examination. Culture obtained; preliminary growth consistent with skin flora. Blood cultures negative. Afebrile throughout observation. Leukocytosis improved without complication.

Treatment: Received wound irrigation and local dressing changes. Started on dicloxacillin with good tolerance. Pain controlled with acetaminophen. No operative debridement required.

Discharge medications:
- Dicloxacillin, continue as prescribed to complete course
- Acetaminophen as needed for wound discomfort

Instructions: Keep dressing clean and dry. Change dressing daily or sooner if saturated. Wash hands before and after wound care. Do not apply peroxide, alcohol, or unprescribed ointments. Return to the ED for fever, rapidly spreading redness, increasing drainage, worsening pain, wound separation, or new weakness.

Condition at discharge: Stable, ambulatory, tolerating oral intake. Friend present for discharge teaching; patient verbalized understanding.

Follow-up: Surgical clinic for wound check and culture review. Follow up with primary care after antibiotic completion. Further management pending final culture results.

Patient: myarii ironwing
MRN: 01277840
Contact: (202) 555-0126

Triage: a 15-year-old South Asian female patient with hemoglobin SS disease presents with severe bilateral leg pain and low back pain since yesterday. Kalki, uncle, at bedside; reports decreased oral intake and dark urine. No chest pain, cough, dyspnea, fever, vomiting, or focal weakness. Patient assents to evaluation and requests uncle remain present.

Exam: Awake, uncomfortable, conversant. Mucous membranes dry. HR 112, BP 118/72, RR 20, SpO2 99% RA, T 37.1 C. Lungs clear, no increased work of breathing. Tachycardic, regular. Abdomen soft, nontender. Diffuse tenderness of thighs and lumbar paraspinal region; no joint erythema or swelling. Neuro intact.

Weight: 54.0 kg

Testing: CBC with Hgb 8.4 g/dL, reticulocyte count 9.8%, WBC 14.2 K/uL, platelets 412 K/uL. CMP notable for total bilirubin 3.1 mg/dL; creatinine 0.7 mg/dL. UA concentrated, negative nitrite. Chest radiograph without infiltrate.

MDM: Findings consistent with uncomplicated vaso-occlusive painful crisis and dehydration. No evidence acute chest syndrome, sepsis, or focal osteomyelitis. IV access obtained. Lactated Ringer’s bolus given, followed by maintenance IV fluids. Morphine administered with improvement from 9/10 to 4/10; repeat dose given, pain now 2/10. Oral fluids tolerated.

Disposition: Discharge with home sickle cell pain plan, hydration, and close hematology follow-up. Return immediately for fever, chest symptoms, dyspnea, worsening pain, or inability to drink. Uncle and patient verbalized understanding.

Continue telemetry, oxygen and pulse-ox monitoring, anticoagulation safety checks, respiratory assessment, assisted ambulation, and intake/output documentation. Reinforce discharge teaching and medication adherence. Cardiology follow-up planned in about 12 weeks.

Referral: Community Pediatrics
SSN: 666-09-4783
Referring organization: Bergen New Bridge Medical Center
Patient: K. Staven
Relative present: daveah fregozo, uncle

Dear Pediatric Pulmonology Team,

I am referring K. Staven, a 16-year-old East Asian female patient, for evaluation after an acute asthma exacerbation with persistent wheeze, increased work of breathing, and night-time cough. The specific question is whether the current symptoms represent poorly controlled asthma requiring a step-up in controller therapy and whether additional pulmonary testing is indicated.

The history was obtained from the patient and daveah fregozo. Symptoms worsened over the past several days, with cough disturbing sleep and intermittent chest tightness. There has been no reported fever, syncope, hemoptysis, or choking episode. The patient is able to speak in full sentences and is drinking normally. No prior intensive care admission is reported. Family is concerned about recurrent symptoms during exercise and at night.

At today’s visit, the patient was alert but mildly tachypneic, with scattered expiratory wheezes and mildly prolonged expiration. Work of breathing improved after albuterol administered through a spacer. Oxygen saturation remained acceptable on room air. There was no focal lung finding, stridor, or cyanosis. The patient and uncle received spacer teaching, including return demonstration and instructions regarding mouthpiece seal, inhalation technique, and cleaning.

Current treatment is albuterol inhaler with spacer as needed. The family was instructed to follow the prescribed rescue-use directions and to seek emergency care for worsening retractions, inability to speak comfortably, cyanosis, poor intake, or inadequate response to albuterol. Please note that the relevant clinician involved in prior respiratory care is described in the record as an attending pulmonologist.

Assessment: Acute asthma exacerbation, improved after bronchodilator treatment, with ongoing nocturnal and exertional symptoms suggesting incomplete control.

Requested action: Please assess asthma severity and control, review inhaler technique and triggers, and advise on controller medication selection, pulmonary function testing, and follow-up interval.

Sincerely,

Yamin Cowick

Pulmonary Medicine Consultation Report

Patient: Beverley
MRN: 037943212
Contact: (202) 555-0178
Encounter date: 02/01/2020

Reason for consultation: Hereditary breast and ovarian cancer risk assessment; significant family history and request for predictive testing.

History: Beverley is a 76-year-old Middle Eastern male patient referred for cancer-risk counseling after learning that a sibling carries a pathogenic BRCA1 c.68_69delAG variant. The patient reports concern about personal cancer risk and asks whether predictive germline testing is appropriate. No current treatment. No acute pulmonary complaints are reported today.

Interpretation: The reported familial variant is clinically significant and, if confirmed in the affected relative, provides a specific target for cascade testing. The patient’s result cannot be inferred from family history alone. Testing should be performed with informed consent and include discussion of possible positive, negative, and uncertain results, as well as implications for surveillance and relatives.

Plan:
1. Obtain the sibling’s genetic test report, including laboratory and variant classification, before ordering targeted testing.
2. Refer to genetic counseling for formal pedigree review, consent, and selection of the appropriate germline assay.
3. Review personal history, ancestry, prior breast or ovarian screening, and reproductive considerations at the genetics visit.
4. Continue routine primary-care preventive care pending results; no pulmonary medication indicated.
5. Patient advised to contact the clinic after the family report is available so testing and follow-up can be coordinated.

LABORATORY REPORT

Patient: Naevia S., a 55-year-old Native American male patient
Specimen: Peripheral blood, EDTA
Test: Hereditary breast and ovarian cancer risk assessment
Report/accession ID: 03998484
Ordering clinician: Not listed
Collection status: Adequate specimen; DNA extracted for targeted hereditary cancer panel

RESULTS
BRCA1 c.68_69delAG: Not detected
BRCA1 sequencing and deletion/duplication analysis: No pathogenic or likely pathogenic variant identified
BRCA2 analysis: No pathogenic or likely pathogenic variant identified
Panel quality: Acceptable; internal controls passed

INTERPRETATION
Negative for the tested familial BRCA1 c.68_69delAG variant and other reportable alterations included on this assay. This result does not eliminate hereditary cancer risk, particularly in the setting of a significant family history or an unrecognized familial variant.

CLINICAL COMMENT
Predictive testing requested because of cancer-risk concern and family history. Results should be interpreted with the family pedigree and, when available, the affected relative’s molecular report. A negative result is most informative when the familial pathogenic variant is established and specifically assessed.

ACTION
— Refer to genetic counseling for individualized residual-risk discussion.
— Continue routine screening based on personal and family history; specialty recommendations may differ from average-risk guidance.
— Follow-up genetics review scheduled for 02/27/2036.

Validated by: Mynor Polder, MD
Final report: Released to ordering clinician.

Date: 1988-03-14
Patient: X. Oxsen   MRN: 09779881
DOB: February 18th, 1908
Contact: (212) 555-0122

Reason for visit: Sleep evaluation.

History:
Loud snoring nightly. Partner reports witnessed pauses in breathing with occasional gasping. Marked daytime somnolence; falls asleep during television and as a passenger. Symptoms present for several months. Nasal congestion for 3 days, without fever or shortness of breath. No prior sleep study documented.

Medications: Continuous positive airway pressure; using inconsistently because of nasal obstruction. No sedative use reported.

Vitals: BP at goal. Pulse regular. BMI elevated. Oropharynx crowded; tonsils not enlarged. Lungs clear bilaterally. Neuro grossly intact.

Assessment:
1. Suspected obstructive sleep apnea, symptomatic.
2. Daytime sleepiness, likely related to untreated sleep-disordered breathing.
3. Acute nasal congestion affecting CPAP tolerance.

Plan:
Sleep medicine referral for diagnostic study and CPAP data download.
Continue CPAP nightly as tolerated; reviewed mask fit and humidification.
Saline nasal spray and intranasal steroid trial for congestion.
Avoid driving when drowsy. Follow up after sleep study or sooner for worsening symptoms.

Electronically signed, Internal Medicine.

Emergency Department Assessment
SSN: 936167213

Patient: SULTAAN CONTARDO
DOB: Jan 19, 2001
Address: 499 State Hwy 156, Arcadia, MO 63621
Encounter date: July 31st, 2035
Historian: Patient; friend at bedside

Chief complaint: Sudden shortness of breath and right-sided chest pain.

History of present illness: Abrupt dyspnea beginning earlier today with sharp right pleuritic pain, worse on deep inspiration. Reports rapid heartbeat and mild lightheadedness. No syncope, hemoptysis, fever, or recent respiratory illness. Friend reports patient appeared pale and anxious at onset. No known prior venous thromboembolism reported.

Initial vital signs: BP 132/84, HR 118, RR 26, SpO2 89% on room air, temperature 98.4°F.

Exam: Alert, anxious, speaking in short sentences. Tachycardic, regular rhythm. Increased work of breathing without wheezing. Lungs clear but diminished at bases. No unilateral leg edema or calf tenderness. Abdomen soft, nontender. Glasgow Coma Scale 15.

Investigations:
- ECG: Sinus tachycardia; no ST-elevation.
- CBC without significant anemia or leukocytosis.
- BMP acceptable; troponin negative.
- CTA chest: Acute segmental pulmonary emboli in the right lower lobe; no CT evidence of right-heart strain.
- Portable chest radiograph without focal infiltrate.

ED course: Supplemental oxygen applied with improvement of saturation to 96%. Hemodynamically stable throughout observation. Apixaban initiated after bleeding-risk review; first dose given in ED.

Assessment: Acute pulmonary embolism without shock or radiographic right-heart strain.

Disposition: Discharge home with anticoagulation instructions and strict return precautions. Follow-up with primary care arranged. Attending: marselo banick

NEONATAL LABORATORY REPORT

Patient: L. Shiffrin
MRN: 0532817
Specimen/Report Date: 09/07/2035
Location: Neonatal intensive care unit
Clinical context: The 2-week-old Native American female neonate is being evaluated for jaundiced skin, sleepy feeding, and reduced intake. Current weight: 3.4 kg. Receiving phototherapy and feeding support.

Specimen: Heel-stick blood, total bilirubin fractionation and basic chemistry.

RESULTS
Total bilirubin: 15.8 mg/dL
Direct bilirubin: 0.4 mg/dL
Indirect bilirubin: 15.4 mg/dL
Hemolysis index: Acceptable
Glucose: 72 mg/dL
Calcium: 9.1 mg/dL
Sodium: 138 mmol/L
Potassium: 5.2 mmol/L
CO2: 22 mmol/L

Reference interpretation:
Total bilirubin is elevated for the laboratory reference interval, with predominantly unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia. Direct bilirubin is not increased. Interpretation of treatment threshold requires correlation with gestational maturity, postnatal age in hours, and neurotoxicity risk factors.

Comment:
Findings support unconjugated neonatal hyperbilirubinemia consistent with the reported jaundice. Continue phototherapy per the neonatal treatment nomogram and clinical protocol. Maintain frequent monitored feeds; follow intake, urine output, and weight trend. Repeat total and direct bilirubin after the next treatment interval or sooner if feeding or clinical status worsens. Consider CBC, reticulocyte count, blood type/direct antiglobulin testing, and G6PD evaluation if bilirubin rises unexpectedly or hemolysis is suspected. Direct bilirubin is currently reassuring against significant cholestasis.

Validated and reported by: Mansoor Samba
Laboratory Medicine/Neonatology

Referral to Endocrinology
SSN: 900-93-3394

Patient: ZAYD LOCURCIO
Employer: Avon Senior Center
Spouse/contact: kimbella odunze

I am referring ZAYD LOCURCIO for evaluation and management of suspected undertreated hypothyroidism. The main concerns are persistent fatigue, marked sensitivity to cold, and constipation. These symptoms have continued despite adherence to levothyroxine as prescribed. The patient reports no recent medication changes and no use of over-the-counter thyroid products.

Recent laboratory testing showed TSH 8.2 mIU/L. I would appreciate your assessment of whether the current levothyroxine regimen is adequate and whether additional thyroid testing or medication counseling is indicated. Please also consider alternative causes of fatigue if the thyroid findings do not fully account for the symptoms.

On review today, the patient appeared tired but was alert and conversant. No acute respiratory distress was observed in the pulmonary clinic. Medication reconciliation was completed, and levothyroxine remains the only thyroid medication reported. Constipation has been managed with increased fluids and dietary fiber, with limited benefit.

Please review administration timing, adherence, drug and supplement interactions, and the need for repeat TSH after any dose adjustment. If treatment is changed, please send recommendations back to our office so monitoring can be coordinated with primary care. The patient understands the reason for referral and agrees with the plan.

Referring clinician: Darianna Bonano
Clinical locality: Peyton

MRN: MRN-00508910
Visit type: Internal medicine follow-up
Clinic: Orange City Area Health System
Occupation: Dental Receptionist

Chief concern: Increased thirst, fatigue, and frequent urination over the past several weeks.

History:
Known type 2 diabetes mellitus. Taking metformin 500 mg twice daily with food and atorvastatin as prescribed. Reports increased intake of water and nocturia; no dysuria, fever, vomiting, or abdominal pain. Fatigue worse late afternoon. Friend present for support. No home glucose log available.

Vitals:
BP 132/78; pulse 84; respirations 16; temperature 98.4°F; SpO2 98% room air.

Exam:
Alert, well appearing. Mucous membranes mildly dry. Heart regular rate and rhythm. Lungs clear. Abdomen soft, nontender. No lower-extremity edema. Foot skin intact; dorsalis pedis pulses palpable bilaterally.

Results:
Point-of-care glucose elevated. Urinalysis with glucosuria, negative ketones and nitrites. Hemoglobin A1c ordered; CMP, urine microalbumin, and fasting lipid panel ordered.

Assessment:
1. Type 2 diabetes mellitus, likely above goal with polyuria and polydipsia.
2. Fatigue, likely metabolic; evaluate renal function and anemia.
3. Hyperlipidemia, on atorvastatin.

Plan:
Continue current medications pending laboratory review. Hydration encouraged. Begin home glucose checks and bring log to follow-up. Diabetic eye exam and nutrition counseling discussed. Return precautions reviewed for vomiting, confusion, or inability to keep fluids down.

Electronically signed by kailah teslow.

Clinical Genetics Referral
SSN: 917-26-8828

Patient: zionna stough
Emergency contact: Sandor Noeth

Dear Clinical Genetics Team,

I am referring zionna stough for assessment of possible inherited cancer susceptibility in the setting of newly confirmed Hodgkin lymphoma. The clinical question is whether the patient’s presentation, together with the available family history, warrants germline testing and tailored counseling regarding recurrence risk and implications for relatives.

The patient initially developed painless lymphadenopathy, followed by drenching night sweats and unintentional weight loss. Excisional lymph-node biopsy confirmed Hodgkin lymphoma. Staging and treatment planning are being coordinated through oncology; current management is supportive care pending tissue diagnosis review. No hereditary testing has yet been completed.

Family history is limited at present. Sandor Noeth, listed as the emergency contact, is assisting with collection of additional information regarding malignancies in first- and second-degree relatives. A three-generation pedigree would be helpful, including hematologic cancers, breast or colorectal cancer, unusually early diagnoses, and multiple primary tumors. Please also review whether the pathology and treatment history suggest a syndrome-associated pattern rather than sporadic disease.

On examination, persistent cervical and supraclavicular adenopathy is documented, without acute respiratory compromise. The patient understands that genetic evaluation may affect relatives and is agreeable to counseling. Please arrange consultation, obtain consent for any indicated germline testing, and provide written guidance on results, limitations, and family communication.

Referring clinician: ARYEL PINKEL, primary care clinician
Service locality: Bloomingrose
Professional ID: 015850399

Sincerely,

ARYEL PINKEL

LABORATORY REPORT

Patient: G. Daughenbaugh
DOB: 07/06/1957
Collection date: August 10, 2035
Report/accession ID: 051183511
Ordering clinician: Not listed
Specimens: EDTA whole blood; plantar wound swab, left foot

Clinical indication:
Diabetes mellitus with plantar ulceration, reduced sensation, and local discharge. Evaluation for glycemic control and wound infection.

RESULTS

Hemoglobin A1c: 8.7%  
Reference interpretation: Above recommended treatment goal for most adults with diabetes; correlate with individualized target and recent glucose history.

WBC: 10.8 x10^3/µL (4.0–10.5)
Hemoglobin: 12.9 g/dL (12.0–16.0)
CRP: 18.6 mg/L (0.0–8.0)

Wound culture:
Moderate growth of Staphylococcus aureus. Susceptibility testing pending.
Gram stain: Moderate polymorphonuclear leukocytes; few gram-positive cocci in clusters.

INTERPRETIVE COMMENT
Elevated A1c indicates suboptimal glycemic control and may impair ulcer healing. Mild leukocytosis and elevated CRP support localized inflammation. Culture findings should be interpreted with depth of specimen and clinical examination; superficial colonization cannot be excluded.

ACTION
— Final organism identification and antimicrobial susceptibilities to follow.
— Correlate with wound appearance, depth, perfusion, and systemic symptoms.
— Continue wound care and amoxicillin-clavulanate pending susceptibility review; reassess therapy when final results are available.
— Consider podiatry/wound-care evaluation for debridement and off-loading.

Validated by: S. Cheeney  
Laboratory clinician

PEDIATRIC ED ASSESSMENT

Patient: Naarah
Guardian/legal decision-maker: Hathaway
The patient, age 7 years, was reviewed with guardian at bedside.

Chief complaint: Right lower-quadrant abdominal pain
Onset: Per guardian, began periumbilically yesterday and migrated to RLQ. Nausea and poor appetite. No reported diarrhea. Last oral intake yesterday evening.

Triage: Afebrile, mildly tachycardic. Pain worse with walking and coughing.
Exam: Alert, uncomfortable with movement. Dry lips. Abdomen soft, focal RLQ tenderness with guarding; positive McBurney tenderness. No generalized rigidity. Lungs clear. Capillary refill <2 sec.

Time of symptom escalation: 08:15.

Investigations:
CBC: Leukocytosis with neutrophil predominance.
CMP: No significant electrolyte abnormality.
Urinalysis: No pyuria or hematuria.
Ultrasound: Noncompressible dilated appendix with periappendiceal inflammatory change, consistent with acute appendicitis.

ED course: NPO. IV fluids given. Acetaminophen administered for pain. Ampicillin-sulbactam started after IV access obtained. Pediatric surgery consulted at Northwestern Medical Center Inc; operative evaluation recommended. Guardian understands findings and agrees with transfer/admission pathway. Assent obtained as appropriate.

Disposition: Stable for admission to pediatric surgery; continue NPO, IV fluids, antibiotics, serial abdominal exams.

Follow-up/review: 2025-02-16 if discharged plan changes or postoperative review is required.

No recent respiratory infection or chest pain. Established obstructive sleep apnea on continuous positive airway pressure. Using device most nights, approximately 6 hours/night; intermittent mask leak.

PAP download: Residual AHI mildly elevated. Adherence below goal. Nocturnal symptoms improved when mask remains sealed.

Vitals: Stable in office. SpO2 normal on room air.
Exam: Alert, tired appearing. Oropharynx crowded. Lungs clear bilaterally. Regular cardiac rhythm. No peripheral edema.

Assessment:
1. Obstructive sleep apnea—partial CPAP adherence, mask fit issue.
2. Daytime somnolence, likely related to suboptimal PAP use.

Plan:
- Replace mask/cushion; review humidification and tubing.
- Continue CPAP nightly and during naps.
- Avoid driving when drowsy.
- Sleep medicine respiratory therapist to review download and settings.
- Follow up in 6–8 weeks or sooner for worsening symptoms.

Signed by: Lewin Pizzoferrato
Mount Desert Island Hospital

Patient: azryah veglahn
Patient context: The patient, age 15 years, was admitted to Northwest Missississippi Regional Medical Center for vaso-occlusive sickle cell painful crisis with severe bilateral limb pain, back pain, and poor oral intake/dehydration.
Family contact: Aunt Kahlea Macheras, from Blue Springs, involved in discharge teaching and transport planning.

Admission findings
- Significant extremity and lumbar pain; dry mucous membranes.
- No fever, chest pain, hypoxia, or focal neurologic deficit.
- Current vital sign: blood pressure 108/66 mmHg.

Hospital course
- Treated with intravenous fluids and scheduled/PRN morphine, followed by transition to oral analgesia as pain improved.
- Encouraged oral hydration; urine output and intake improved.
- CBC and reticulocyte count consistent with known sickle cell disease. Chest radiograph without acute infiltrate. No transfusion indicated.
- Pain decreased to tolerable level, ambulating independently, tolerating meals and fluids. No development of acute chest syndrome or infection.

Medication changes at discharge
- Continue home sickle cell medications as previously prescribed.
- Oral opioid analgesic for breakthrough pain per discharge medication list; avoid duplicate acetaminophen-containing products.
- Continue hydration plan. No antibiotics.

Disposition: Home with aunt after patient assent and guardian discharge discussion. Condition stable.

Follow-up/actions
- Hematology follow-up with Northwest Missississippi Regional Medical Center; primary care appointment to be arranged.
- Return to ED for fever, breathing difficulty, chest pain, worsening pain unresponsive to medication, persistent vomiting, or inability to drink.
- Written crisis plan reviewed with patient and aunt; questions answered.

Patient: A. Friedges
SSN: 966 49 0412
DOB: April 27th, 2026
Accompanied by father, Konstantina

Emergency Department Assessment

Brought in for cough, noisy breathing, and decreased feeding for 3 days. Father reports nasal congestion with intermittent subcostal pulling, worse overnight. Fewer ounces taken today but still making wet diapers. No apnea, cyanosis, vomiting, or known sick contacts. Immunizations reported current.

On arrival, infant awake and consolable. Mild tachypnea with occasional subcostal retractions. Nasal congestion and transmitted upper-airway sounds present. No grunting or head bobbing. Breath sounds coarse and mildly diminished at the bases but without focal crackles or wheezing. Heart rate regular, capillary refill less than 2 seconds. Mucous membranes moist. Abdomen soft and nondistended.

Respiratory viral testing was not pursued because the result would not change management. After nasal suctioning and saline, breathing effort improved and the infant took a supervised oral feed without choking or emesis. Oxygen saturation remained appropriate on room air during observation.

Assessment: Clinical bronchiolitis with mild increased work of breathing and reduced intake. No current indication for supplemental oxygen, IV fluids, bronchodilator therapy, or antibiotics.

Plan: Discharge home with supportive care, frequent smaller feeds, and nasal saline as needed followed by gentle suctioning. Father instructed to return for persistent increased work of breathing, pauses in breathing, blue discoloration, inability to feed, or markedly fewer wet diapers. Follow-up arranged with MERCY MEDICAL CENTER-NEW HAMPTON on 09/23/2026; pediatrician follow-up sooner if symptoms worsen. Father verbalized understanding and agrees with the plan.

Julliette Deprato

Clinical Genetics Laboratory Report

Patient: A. Cina
DOB: April 10, 1949
MRN: 086619988
Specimen: Peripheral blood, EDTA
Ordering clinician: Not listed
Indication: Hypothyroidism with fatigue, cold intolerance, and constipation; treated with levothyroxine.

Results:
TSH: 8.2 mIU/L (reference interval 0.40–4.50 mIU/L) — high
Free T4: 0.8 ng/dL (reference interval 0.8–1.8 ng/dL) — low-normal
Thyroid peroxidase antibody: 186 IU/mL (reference value <9 IU/mL) — positive
Thyroglobulin antibody: 32 IU/mL (reference value ≤1 IU/mL) — positive

Molecular analysis:
Targeted sequencing of the TSH receptor, PAX8, TTF2, and associated congenital hypothyroidism genes identified no pathogenic or likely pathogenic variant. No copy-number alteration was detected by the assay. This result does not exclude regulatory, deep intronic, mitochondrial, or other variants outside the regions assessed.

Interpretation:
The biochemical profile demonstrates suboptimal thyroid hormone replacement, with elevated TSH and low-normal free T4. Positive thyroid autoantibodies support autoimmune thyroiditis as the most likely etiology. The negative molecular findings do not alter the current clinical interpretation and should not be used to discontinue levothyroxine.

Clinical comment:
Correlate with adherence, administration timing, interacting medications or supplements, and recent dose changes. Medication adjustment should be managed by the treating clinician; repeat thyroid function testing is reasonable after dose stabilization.

Follow-up review: February 15th, 2036

Validated and reported by: Sua Millington, MD

Pulmonary Medicine Referral
SSN: 000-30-7441

To: Pulmonary Medicine Service

Re: Kearis Moges
Report/accession ID: 018519357

Dear Specialist,

I am referring Kearis Moges for expedited pulmonary and tissue-diagnosis evaluation. The patient has several weeks of painless lymphadenopathy, drenching night sweats, and unintentional weight loss. Examination in primary care demonstrates firm, nontender cervical and supraclavicular nodes without overlying erythema. Breath sounds are clear bilaterally, with no resting respiratory distress. No current fever was recorded.

Chest imaging obtained during the initial workup shows mediastinal and bilateral hilar adenopathy, with additional cervical adenopathy. The clinical picture is concerning for Hodgkin lymphoma, although metastatic disease, infection, and other lymphoproliferative disorders remain in the differential. CBC demonstrates mild normocytic anemia; renal and hepatic function are adequate for further diagnostic evaluation. No tissue diagnosis has yet been obtained.

Current management is supportive care pending tissue diagnosis, including oral hydration, nutritional support, and symptom monitoring. Please assess for the safest and most informative biopsy approach, including whether bronchoscopic sampling or another pulmonary procedure is appropriate. Please also advise regarding baseline pulmonary testing before definitive treatment and coordinate with hematology/oncology after pathology is available.

The patient and spouse understand the concern and the need for prompt specialty evaluation. Follow-up with our office is scheduled for April 6, 2019.

Referring clinician: RUSHDA VANFOSSEN
UNIVERSITY OF MISSISSIPPI MEDICAL CENTER- GRENADA

Date: 2028-05-09

Dear Behavioral Health Consultant,

I am referring Borja for evaluation and treatment recommendations regarding persistent anxiety despite an initial primary care medication trial. Borja reports excessive worry on most days, difficulty quieting thoughts at bedtime, and shoulder and jaw muscle tension. Sleep is generally poor, with prolonged sleep onset and intermittent nighttime awakening. Symptoms have begun to interfere with concentration and usual work responsibilities.

Occupation: Dental Receptionist
Address: 271 Canebrake Rd, Sandstone, WV 25985
Emergency contact: Relative listed in the chart.

There is no reported history of manic symptoms, psychosis, or prior psychiatric hospitalization. The patient denies current suicidal intent or plan. Appetite is stable. Office examination was notable for an anxious affect and mild trapezius tension; speech was organized, and insight was intact. No acute medical findings were identified to account for the presentation.

Current medication: sertraline 50 mg once daily. The medication has been taken consistently, with mild early nausea that has resolved. Benefit remains limited, and the patient would like guidance before any dose change. We reviewed sleep routine, reduction of evening caffeine, and use of brief diaphragmatic-breathing exercises.

Assessment: Generalized anxiety disorder with persistent worry, insomnia, and muscle tension; partial response to sertraline.

Please assess diagnostic and treatment options, including psychotherapy recommendations and whether medication adjustment is appropriate. A written consultation plan would be appreciated.

Sincerely,

SAELAH BUHL

Collection: Midstream urine; adequate volume
Ordering clinician: Not listed

Color: Amber
Appearance: Cloudy

Nitrite: Positive
Protein: 2+
Blood: 2+
Glucose: Negative
Ketones: Trace

Microscopy
WBC: >100/hpf
RBC: 20–50/hpf
Bacteria: Many

Date: 10/05/2022
Patient: FAIZAH EDEN
MRN: 0851967
Accompanied by friend: CIERAN ADEWOLE

Chief complaint: Increasing redness and pain, left lower leg.

HPI: Spreading erythema over 2 days with local warmth and leg tenderness. No reported trauma, drainage, chest pain, or dyspnea. Current pain 5/10. No prior treatment before arrival.

Vitals: Stable; afebrile. Oxygenation normal on room air.
Exam: Nontoxic appearance. Approximate 12-cm area of blanching erythema and warmth over anterior distal left lower leg. Tender to palpation. No fluctuance, crepitus, lymphangitic streaking, or open wound. Calf compartments soft. Distal pulses and sensation intact.

Investigations:
CBC without leukocytosis. BMP without acute abnormality.
Venous duplex, left leg: no DVT.
Bedside soft-tissue ultrasound: cobblestoning; no drainable collection.

Assessment: Cellulitis of lower leg. No abscess, necrotizing infection, or venous thrombosis identified.

Treatment/MDM: First dose dicloxacillin given in ED. Acetaminophen for pain. Outpatient therapy appropriate given stable examination and reliable follow-up. Case reviewed with Northern Light Mayo Hospital.

Disposition: Discharge home. Continue dicloxacillin as prescribed and acetaminophen as needed. Elevate leg; return for fever, rapid spread, severe pain, drainage, or systemic symptoms. Recheck with primary care in 24–48 hours.

DISCHARGE SUMMARY
SSN: 666 55 1027

Patient: Hazlee Sacchi
Admission/discharge date: Jan 6, 2019
Service: Clinical Genetics
Attending: Mount Pleasant Hospital

Reason for admission:
Acute pulmonary embolism with sudden breathlessness, pleuritic chest pain, and tachycardia. Presented to ED requiring supplemental oxygen.

Key results:
CTA chest positive for segmental pulmonary emboli. No right-heart strain on imaging. Troponin negative. Lower-extremity venous ultrasound without DVT. Hemodynamically stable throughout admission.

Hospital course:
Started on anticoagulation with apixaban. Oxygen weaned to room air before discharge. Pleuritic discomfort improved; heart rate normalized. No bleeding, syncope, or recurrent hypoxemia. Clinical genetics reviewed family history and recommended outpatient thrombophilia/genetic risk assessment after the acute event; testing deferred during anticoagulation.

Discharge medications:
- apixaban 5 mg twice daily
- Acetaminophen as needed for pain
- Supplemental oxygen: not required at discharge

Condition:
Alert, ambulatory, tolerating diet, room-air saturation stable. Discharge home with friend, Sailor Potapchuk, in Aiken.

Follow-up/actions:
- Follow up with Mount Pleasant Hospital and primary care for anticoagulation management.
- Hematology/genetics clinic referral for unprovoked PE evaluation.
- Avoid NSAIDs unless specifically cleared.
- Seek emergency care for worsening shortness of breath, chest pain, fainting, coughing blood, or significant bleeding.

Medication counseling completed; patient verbalized understanding.

Three days of worsening wheeze with increased work of breathing and nighttime cough. Used albuterol inhaler more frequently than usual with temporary relief. No fever, vomiting, or known foreign-body event. Uncle reports missed controller doses this week. Patient assents to examination and treatment discussion; uncle present and participates in plan.

Alert, speaking in full sentences. Mild nasal flaring and intercostal retractions. Diffuse expiratory wheezes, decreased air movement at bases. No cyanosis. Heart regular. Oropharynx clear.

Acute asthma exacerbation, likely triggered by viral upper respiratory illness and inconsistent controller use. No current indication for ED transfer; reassess after bronchodilator.

Treatment/action:
Albuterol nebulizer administered in clinic with improved aeration and reduced work of breathing. Reviewed albuterol inhaler and spacer teaching; patient demonstrated technique correctly. Continue rescue albuterol per asthma action plan. Oral steroid course prescribed. Resume daily controller as previously directed.

Follow-up:
Return for worsening respiratory effort, inability to speak comfortably, poor response to albuterol, or cyanosis. Follow up with primary care within 48–72 hours. Family advised to schedule review with the attending pulmonologist.

Documented by astor ortizmartinez, pediatric clinic clinician.

Cardiology Referral

Patient: Arland
Report/accession ID: 0973747515
Referring organization: ROPER HOSPITAL

Dear Cardiology Colleague,

I am referring Arland for assessment of intermittent palpitations and exertional fatigue in the setting of treated hypothyroidism. The specific question is whether the reported episodes represent a clinically significant arrhythmia and whether additional cardiac evaluation is indicated.

The patient’s partner reports approximately 6 weeks of episodic “fluttering” sensations, occurring at rest and occasionally with brisk activity, without syncope, chest pain, or sustained dyspnea. Fatigue, cold intolerance, and constipation have also persisted despite adherence to levothyroxine. No stimulant or energy-drink use reported. Family cardiac history was not available at this visit.

Office examination: BP 118/72 mmHg, pulse 84/min and regular, oxygen saturation 98% on room air. Heart sounds normal without murmur; lungs clear; no peripheral edema. ECG in the office showed sinus rhythm without acute ST-T changes.

Recent laboratory testing showed TSH 6.8 mIU/L with free T4 0.9 ng/dL. Medication: levothyroxine 75 micrograms once daily. The thyroid replacement dose has not yet been adjusted pending review of the palpitations and laboratory trend.

Please evaluate for ambulatory rhythm monitoring and advise regarding any cardiac contribution to the fatigue. Recommendations for coordination of thyroid management would also be appreciated.

Sincerely,

Suhaira Bago, 074733371
Referring clinician

SSN: 960-90-4449

To: Sleep Medicine Service

Re: Lukka B.

Dear Sleep Medicine Clinician,

I am referring Lukka B. for evaluation and management of probable obstructive sleep apnea. The patient reports loud snoring most nights, and a sibling has repeatedly observed pauses in breathing followed by gasping during sleep. There is prominent daytime somnolence, including difficulty staying alert during routine activities. The patient presented to the emergency department after a recent episode of falling asleep unexpectedly during the day. They also report cough for 3 days, without respiratory distress or fever.

In the ED, the patient was awake and conversant. Respirations were even, with clear breath sounds and no hypoxia on routine observation. The oropharyngeal examination suggested a crowded airway. No acute cardiopulmonary process was identified, and discharge was appropriate. The patient has previously been advised to use continuous positive airway pressure but has not yet had formal sleep-medicine follow-up or documented adherence assessment. No new sedating medication was started.

Assessment: Symptoms and witnessed apneas are concerning for clinically significant obstructive sleep apnea with excessive daytime sleepiness. The acute cough appears unrelated and is being managed conservatively.

Plan/request: Please arrange diagnostic sleep testing, review candidacy and tolerance for positive airway pressure therapy, and assess whether equipment settings require adjustment. Guidance regarding driving and other activities affected by somnolence would also be appreciated. Follow-up is requested on 2045-12-22.

Referring organization: West Tennessee Healthcare Bolivar Hospital
Report/accession ID: S22-0093695

Sincerely,

C. Fileccia

Patient: JAYLON GRATTAN
Home address: 477 Missle Rd, Lander, WY 82520
Patient contact: (617) 555-0111

You were admitted after a brief episode of right arm weakness, left facial droop, and slurred speech. The symptoms resolved before discharge. Your sibling provided additional history and confirmed that you returned to your usual function.

Brain imaging showed no acute infarct or hemorrhage. Vascular imaging did not show a large-vessel blockage. Cardiac monitoring remained in sinus rhythm, and the echocardiogram did not identify a clear embolic source. Laboratory testing was reviewed without an acute explanation for the event. The overall assessment is transient ischemic attack (TIA).

Treatment during admission included aspirin and initiation/continuation of atorvastatin for vascular risk reduction. Continue the discharge medicines exactly as listed on your medication bottle and medication list. Do not stop aspirin or atorvastatin without speaking with your primary care clinician or neurology. Arrange primary care and neurology follow-up in 20 days for blood pressure, cholesterol, medication tolerance, and further stroke-risk planning.

Call 911 immediately for new weakness or numbness, facial droop, trouble speaking, vision loss, severe sudden headache, chest pain, or loss of balance, even if symptoms improve.

text:
Internal Medicine Clinic Consultation

Patient: Bayla Stambaugh
MRN: 02081238
Occupation: Bread Baker
Referring/Primary Care Organization: Maui Memorial Medical Center
Date: Not recorded

Reason for consultation: Pruritic erythematous rash with localized skin irritation.

History and examination:
The patient reports several days of itching and redness affecting the volar forearms and lower neck after use of a newly introduced fragranced personal-care product. No fever, facial swelling, dyspnea, mucosal lesions, drainage, or rapidly progressive pain. Emergency contact is listed in the chart.

Examination shows well-demarcated erythematous, mildly scaly plaques with excoriations in the reported distribution. No vesicles, pustules, cellulitic streaking, fluctuance, or mucosal involvement. The remainder of the visible skin examination is unremarkable. Clinical photographs were reviewed during the visit.

Interpretation:
Findings are most consistent with allergic contact dermatitis. The sharply localized distribution and temporal relationship to a new topical exposure favor contact allergy over urticaria, tinea, or bacterial infection. There is no current evidence of systemic allergic reaction or secondary infection.

Use bland emollient and fragrance-free cleanser. Dermatology referral or patch testing if recurrent, extensive, or persistent despite avoidance. Seek urgent evaluation for facial or tongue swelling, breathing difficulty, fever, or rapidly spreading redness.

Bacteria: Many

Pediatric Discharge Summary
SSN: 666-24-7359

Patient: MAYELIN KRAINZ | 6 y/o
Legal guardian: R. Chalifour, Washington
Service: Pediatrics
Facility: Howard University Hospital Corp

Reason for admission:
Vaso-occlusive sickle cell pain crisis with severe bilateral limb pain, low back pain, and dehydration. Guardian reported cough for 3 days before presentation.

Key results:
Hemoglobin near patient baseline. Reticulocyte count elevated as expected. No focal infiltrate on chest radiograph. Blood cultures negative. Electrolytes improved with hydration.

Hospital course:
Admitted for IV analgesia and rehydration. Morphine initially scheduled, then spaced and transitioned to oral pain medication as symptoms improved. Intravenous fluids administered; oral intake increased. Remained afebrile on room air. No acute chest findings, neurologic changes, or transfusion requirement. Ambulating prior to discharge.

Discharge condition:
Pain controlled on oral regimen. Tolerating fluids and diet. Urine output adequate. Guardian/legal decision-maker present for discharge teaching and assent discussion.

Discharge medications:
Continue home sickle cell medications.
Acetaminophen and ibuprofen as directed for mild pain.
Use prescribed oral opioid only for severe breakthrough pain; no driving or sedating medicines.
Avoid dehydration and strenuous exertion during recovery.

Follow-up:
Primary care and hematology follow-up through Howard University Hospital Corp. Return to ED for fever, chest pain, breathing difficulty, uncontrolled pain, persistent vomiting, or reduced urination.

NURSING PROGRESS NOTE – Pulmonary Medicine

Patient: KENDRELL ENRIGHT
MRN: 048594087
Home address: 420 State Rd 299, Wilmington, DE 19808
Review: the patient, age 61 years, was assessed on morning rounds.
Documenting nurse professional ID: 054239184

Time: 08:15

Assessment:
Severe bilateral lower-extremity and low-back pain, rated 9/10; guarding with repositioning. Awake, oriented, anxious with movement. Skin warm and dry; oral mucosa dry. No chest pain or respiratory distress. Peripheral pulses palpable, no new focal swelling. Known sickle cell painful crisis.

Mobility/Intake:
Remains in bed; requires one-person assist to bedside commode because of pain and weakness. Limited oral intake overnight; sipping water when prompted. Urine concentrated, output reduced per overnight report.

Interventions:
IV fluids continued per order. Morphine administered for breakthrough pain; reassessed after medication. Warm packs applied to back and legs. Encouraged small, frequent oral fluids and assisted repositioning. Fall precautions in place; call light within reach.

Response:
Pain decreased to 6/10 on reassessment, able to rest briefly. No sedation or respiratory rate decline observed. IV site patent without redness or swelling.

Risks/Escalation:
Monitor for worsening pain, hypoxia, fever, acute chest symptoms, and decreased urine output. Covering provider notified of persistent pain and poor intake; request for additional pain-management review pending.

Next shift plan:
Continue ordered fluids and analgesia, document intake/output and response, encourage mobility as tolerated, maintain warming measures and safety precautions. Reassess promptly for respiratory or neurologic change.

Next shift: Continue q4h vitals, stool/emesis count, diaper checks, and parent updates.

Home address: 742 Higginbotham Hwy, Dry Prong, LA 71423

Patient admitted for infectious gastroenteritis with frequent loose stools, vomiting, and intermittent abdominal cramps. Reports diarrhea for 3 days with reduced appetite. Friend, ARIELLAH MICHELETTO, present at bedside and assisting with history. No chest pain or dyspnea reported. Patient states dizziness occurs briefly when standing.

Assessment: Alert and able to answer questions appropriately. Mucous membranes mildly dry. Abdomen soft with mild diffuse cramping; no guarding. Two loose stools and one small emesis during this shift. Urine output decreased but patient has voided once. Peripheral IV remains patent. Interventions: Oral rehydration solution offered in small, frequent amounts and tolerated better than plain water. Ondansetron administered as required for nausea with good effect; no further vomiting for the remainder of the observation period. Assisted to bathroom with one staff member; gait steady after sitting at bedside first. Fall precautions maintained, call light within reach, and intake/output documented. Franklin Medical Center contacted previously regarding the current treatment plan; no new orders received.

Plan for next shift: Continue oral rehydration solution, monitor stool and emesis frequency, reassess abdominal discomfort and orthostatic symptoms, and encourage gradual advancement of diet as tolerated. Notify the covering provider for persistent vomiting, worsening pain, inability to maintain fluids, reduced urine output, fever, or any change in cardiac status.

Patient: Marques, age 22 years
Home address: 125 S Market St, Fresno, CA 93705
Patient contact: (617) 555-0148
Report/accession ID: S28-0563971

Chief complaint: Persistent vomiting in early pregnancy.

History: Presents with sibling for 5 days of worsening nausea and vomiting, unable to tolerate food and limited fluids. Reports dizziness on standing, dry mouth, and approximately 6-lb weight loss by home scale. No abdominal pain, vaginal bleeding, fever, diarrhea, chest pain, or dyspnea. Current pregnancy documented at 9+4 weeks' gestation. Has been taking doxylamine-pyridoxine with incomplete relief. No prior ED treatment this pregnancy.

Exam:
General—tired appearing, alert, cooperative.
Vitals—tachycardic on arrival; blood pressure preserved, afebrile.
Mucous membranes dry. No scleral icterus.
Cardiac regular tachycardia; lungs clear bilaterally.
Abdomen soft, nondistended, nontender, no guarding.
No focal neurologic deficit.

Results:
Urinalysis: concentrated urine, ketones 3+, no nitrites or blood.
BMP: mild hypokalemia; creatinine normal; bicarbonate mildly decreased.
CBC without significant anemia or leukocytosis.
Obstetric ultrasound: single intrauterine pregnancy with cardiac activity, no acute pelvic abnormality.

Assessment: First-trimester hyperemesis with dehydration and weight loss. No evidence of surgical abdomen or infection.

Treatment/Action: Intravenous sodium chloride administered; antiemetic given with improved oral tolerance and heart rate. Potassium replacement provided. Discussed dietary progression, medication use, and return precautions with patient and sibling. Discharged home with prompt obstetric follow-up; admission not required after clinical improvement.

SSN: 666 89 1939

Patient: aiylah pavelchak
Home address: 300 Texas Palmyra Hwy, Houston, PA 15342
Clinical age: 37 y/o
Report/accession ID: 02187065

Presentation: Arrived with acute flank pain, dysuria, chills/rigors, and nausea. Suspected acute pyelonephritis. Awake, conversant, uncomfortable with movement. Skin warm; intermittent shaking chills reported before arrival.

Assessment:
Pain 5/10, left flank, intermittently radiating toward lower abdomen. Dysuria persists. Oral intake limited to sips of water; no emesis in ED. Ambulates slowly to bathroom with standby assistance. Urine specimen obtained and sent; results pending. Peripheral IV patent. Fall precautions in place due to weakness and dizziness when standing.

Interventions/response:
Acetaminophen administered per MAR with partial pain improvement. Cefuroxime given as ordered; no rash, wheezing, or infusion reaction observed. Encouraged oral fluids as tolerated. Warm blanket provided for rigors. Repeat temperature and vital signs monitored; covering provider updated regarding persistent flank pain and limited intake.

Risk/escalation: Monitor for recurrent rigors, hypotension, worsening pain, vomiting, or inability to tolerate oral medication. Escalate promptly for altered mentation or decreased urine output.

Plan for next shift:
Reassess pain, temperature, hydration, and gait. Review urine and laboratory results when available. Continue cefuroxime and acetaminophen as ordered. Maintain assisted toileting and reassess disposition after provider review.

Medication: cefuroxime; acetaminophen.
Documented by covering RN, professional ID 038682143.

EMERGENCY DEPARTMENT ASSESSMENT

Patient: Shivaay
DOB: July 6, 1966
Encounter date: Jan 2, 2026
Department: Clinical Genetics / Emergency Assessment
Healthcare organization: Multicare Auburn Medical Center
Emergency contact: Relative, contact information on file

Chief concern:
Decreased urine output with fatigue and poor oral intake for approximately 2 days. Referred for urgent evaluation after outpatient laboratory concern.

History:
Patient reports minimal urine today, dark in color. No chest pain, dyspnea, flank trauma, or persistent vomiting. Medication reconciliation completed; temporary medication hold advised pending renal recovery.

Exam:
Tired appearing, conversant, mucous membranes dry. BP stable, mild tachycardia. Lungs clear bilaterally. Regular heart rhythm. Abdomen soft, nontender, no guarding. No peripheral edema. Bladder scan without significant retention.

Investigations:
CMP: creatinine 2.1 mg/dL, BUN elevated; electrolytes without emergent abnormality.
Urinalysis: concentrated urine, trace protein, no convincing infection.
CBC without leukocytosis. ECG: sinus rhythm.

Problem / Result / Action:
Acute kidney injury, likely prerenal in setting of reduced intake.
— IV sodium chloride initiated; monitored response and urine output.
— Hold potentially nephrotoxic or blood-pressure-lowering medication temporarily; avoid NSAIDs.
— Repeat metabolic panel after fluids: renal function improving but not yet at baseline.

Disposition:
Admission offered for continued hydration and laboratory monitoring; patient accepted. Nephrology consultation requested. Genetics team notified because of ongoing specialty follow-up. Care transferred to inpatient service.

Documented by: M. Fraijo, Emergency Clinician

Patient: FINNEGAN DACUMOS
Clinical age: 4 y/o
MRN: 015 356 818
Parent present: hanani labranche

Thank you for bringing your child to the pediatric clinic today. The rash and examination are consistent with atopic eczema, with dry, inflamed patches and scratch marks mainly at the elbows, behind the knees, and on the cheeks. The itching has been disturbing sleep. There is no fever, drainage, or evidence of bacterial infection. Parent reports itching and worsening dryness for 3 days.

Please apply the emollient generously to all dry skin at least twice daily and immediately after bathing. Use lukewarm water, keep baths brief, and avoid fragranced soaps, lotions, and detergents. For red or itchy areas, apply the prescribed topical hydrocortisone in a thin layer twice daily for up to 7 days, stopping sooner when the inflammation settles. Do not apply it to the eyes, mouth, or broken skin unless specifically directed. Continue moisturizer even when the skin looks clear.

Trim fingernails and consider cotton pajamas at night to reduce scratching. Call the office for spreading redness, warmth, pus, fever, or worsening pain. We will reassess if sleep remains affected or the rash does not improve after this treatment.

Patient occupation: not applicable for this child.

Sincerely,

Pearla Kisslinger, MD
Pediatric primary care clinician

DISCHARGE SUMMARY
SSN: 000-13-7704

Patient: BARAA TAPANG, 76 y/o patient
Admission/Discharge date: 02/09/2045
Service: Pulmonary Medicine
Emergency contact: Sibling, Hunter Pellettieri, residing in Erath

Reason for admission:
Increasing erythema, purulent drainage, and localized pain at the postoperative incision. No respiratory decompensation.

Key findings:
Afebrile on arrival. Incision with 2-cm area of surrounding erythema and scant purulence; no fascial separation. WBC mildly elevated. Wound culture obtained; final result pending at discharge.
Current vitals: 120/80 mmHg.

Hospital course:
Bedside wound evaluation and irrigation performed. Small superficial opening gently probed; no deep collection identified. Pain improved with acetaminophen. Pulmonary status remained stable on room air. No evidence of systemic infection.

Discharge medications:
Dicloxacillin 500 mg by mouth four times daily for 7 days.
Acetaminophen as needed for incisional pain.
Continue local wound irrigation with clean technique and dry dressing changes.

Condition:
Stable; tolerating diet and ambulating independently. Incision with less erythema and no active purulent drainage at discharge.

Follow-up:
Surgical clinic for wound check within 3–5 days. Primary care follow-up after antibiotic course. Return to ED for fever, spreading redness, worsening pain, recurrent drainage, dyspnea, or other acute concern.

Patient and sibling instructed; understanding confirmed.

Patient: Kaitlin
Occupation: Architectural Drafter
Employer: Hagåtña Housing Authority
Home address: 896 Jalaguac Way, Hagåtña, GU 96910
Patient contact: (671) 555-0153

Chief concern: Increased breathlessness x 4 days with wheeze and thicker yellow sputum. Spouse present; corroborates reduced activity and nighttime cough.

History: COPD with prior exacerbations. Using albuterol inhaler several times daily with temporary relief. No chest pain, syncope, or hemoptysis. No reported fever.

Exam:
BP stable per intake.
General: Mild respiratory distress with exertion; speaking full sentences.
Lungs: Expiratory wheezes bilaterally, diminished air movement at bases.
CV: Regular rate and rhythm.
O2 saturation acceptable on room air at rest.

Assessment: Acute exacerbation of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, likely infectious given purulent sputum. No current findings requiring ED transfer.

Treatment: prednisone 40 mg once daily for 5 days. Doxycycline course prescribed. Continue albuterol inhaler as rescue therapy; review inhaler technique today.

Plan: Increase fluids and rest. Return or call for worsening dyspnea, inability to speak comfortably, cyanosis, confusion, or poor response to rescue inhaler. Follow up with pulmonary clinic after treatment; consider maintenance inhaler review and spirometry when back to baseline.

DISCHARGE SUMMARY
SSN: 666454890

Patient: Matti C.
Service: Clinical Genetics / Women’s Health
Discharge disposition: Home with spouse

Reason for admission:
Acute lower abdominal pain, abnormal vaginal discharge, and dyspareunia. Clinical picture consistent with pelvic inflammatory disease.

Key results:
Pelvic examination with cervical motion and bilateral adnexal tenderness. Pregnancy test negative. NAAT for gonorrhea/chlamydia pending at discharge. CBC without leukocytosis. Pain score 5/10 on arrival.

Hospital course:
Evaluated by gynecology at CHICOT MEMORIAL MEDICAL CENTER. Treated empirically for PID with ceftriaxone administered in the ED, then doxycycline and metronidazole. Symptoms improved; tolerating oral intake and ambulating independently. No fever or hemodynamic instability. No operative intervention indicated.

Discharge medications:
Doxycycline 100 mg by mouth twice daily to complete 14 days.
Metronidazole 500 mg by mouth twice daily to complete 14 days.
Avoid alcohol while taking metronidazole. Complete the full antibiotic course.

Counseling:
No sexual activity until treatment is completed, symptoms have resolved, and partners have been evaluated/treated. Spouse Crissy available for discharge teaching; emergency contact locality documented as Gould.

Follow-up:
Primary care and gynecology review on February 18th, 2023. Return for worsening pain, fever, vomiting, syncope, or inability to take medications.

Condition at discharge: Stable.
